detail.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) continues to influence educational practices and the development of knowledge, with a high level of engagement recorded for younger students, particularly through their active engagement with digital technologies. This study explores the awareness of AI among college students, particularly in Northeastern India through a survey-based approach. A questionnaire was designed drawing on conceptual discussions of technology acceptance, digital inequality, and algorithmic bias. Responses from around 125 students indicate a high level of awareness and many students reporting frequent use of AI tools in their academic work. While many respondents perceive AI as a useful aid for accessing information and supporting learning, others express concern that such tools may be used as shortcuts for completing assignments rather than encouraging deeper academic engagement which may diminish the overall impact of academic coursework. To extend the analysis beyond descriptive statistics, the study introduces an exploratory Artificial Intelligence Perception Index (AIPE), constructed from Likert-scale responses to generate deeper analytical insights. The findings highlight the complex role of AI in academic environments and raise important questions about technological inclusivity and regional representation within emerging digital knowledge systems. At the same time, emerging research suggests that excessive reliance on AI-assisted tools may influence students' independent cognitive skills and critical thinking practices, making it important to critically evaluate how such technologies are integrated into learning environments, particularly within the socio-cultural context of Northeastern India.

detail.title: The Mirror Effect: How Generative AI Exposes the Proxy Architecture of Institutional Accountability

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical framework, the Mirror Effect, for understanding how generative artificial intelligence exposes pre-existing weaknesses in institutional accountability systems rather than creating novel ones. The core thesis is that institutions have historically relied on production scarcity as a heuristic proxy for competence: the difficulty of producing high-quality outputs served as an implicit verification mechanism. Generative AI collapses the cost of plausible output generation to near zero, severing the correlation between observable output quality and genuine understanding. The framework identifies three interconnected dynamics: Proxy Collapse, where traditional signals of competence lose discriminative power; Generation-Verification Asymmetry, where output scales computationally while verification remains cognitively bottlenecked; and Coupled Feedback Loops, where human cognitive biases interact with the sycophantic tendencies of RLHF-trained models to produce selfreinforcing epistemic failures. Mapping institutional governance onto a bias-variance decomposition, the paper characterises the viable governance space as a narrowing corridor between the high-bias failure of over-trusting AI and the high-variance failure of paralysis through over-verification. Cross-sector analysis is presented across higher education, financial services, healthcare, and legal contexts, including the emerging verification escalation posed by agentic AI systems. The paper concludes with boundary conditions, an empirical research agenda, and implications for institutional design.

title: DeepConnect: Harnessing AI to Elevate Collective Human Potential AI as Shared Connective Infrastructure for Collective Sensemaking and Prudent Execution

detail.title: DeepConnect: Harnessing AI to Elevate Collective Human Potential AI as Shared Connective Infrastructure for Collective Sensemaking and Prudent Execution
detail.abstract: Frontier innovation is increasingly constrained not by individual productivity, but by the ability of diverse experts to align meaning, integrate partial views, and translate collectively validated ideas into responsible execution under uncertainty. Yet the dominant adoption pattern for generative AI-private, individualized assistants-risks fragmenting shared mental models and quietly increasing semantic drift across teams. This paper names that failure mode the private-assistant trap: individuals accelerate locally while teams drift globally. This vision paper proposes DeepConnect, a sociotechnical framework and research agenda that deploys AI as shared connective infrastructure. Rather than automating tasks in isolation, DeepConnect serves as a semantic and social bridge that supports collective sensemaking in group-visible contexts. The framework is organized around a People-Ideas-Execution loop and instantiated through two core programs: Synapse (a hybrid knowledge-graph and reasoning engine for interdisciplinary discovery and boundary-object maintenance) and AI Prudent Technologies (APT) (modular, governable "AI boxes" designed for resource-aware, right-sized execution). Recognizing that collective intelligence is an institutional capability rather than a mere software feature, this paper introduces the Collective Needs Ladder to evaluate institutional readiness. It specifies the governance requirements (trust, provenance, contribution valuation) and cultural requirements (psychological safety, cognitive diversity) necessary for durable impact, and offers a research and implementation agenda for AI-enabled collective intelligence at institutional scale.

detail.abstract: India's implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in July 2017 was a watershed moment in the nation's indirect tax history, consolidating a fragmented, multi-tier levy structure into a single, destination-based consumption tax. Despite considerable administrative achievements in formalising the economy and broadening the tax base, empirical evidence regarding the reform's implications for household welfare, purchasing power, and Cost of living remains inconclusive and contested. detail.abstract: Consumer satisfaction and loyalty are pivotal strategic outcomes in the competitive Indian ecommerce market. This study investigates overall consumer satisfaction levels and loyalty intentions for Amazon and Flipkart-India's two dominant e-commerce platforms-and examines how service quality perceptions drive these outcomes. Primary data were collected from 150 active online shoppers through a structured questionnaire and analysed using percentage analysis, one-way ANOVA, and simple linear regression. Findings indicate that 82.0% of Amazon users reported being satisfied or highly satisfied, compared to 66.7% for Flipkart-a gap of 15.3 percentage points. Amazon users also exhibited substantially higher loyalty intentions: 80% would recommend the platform (vs. 63% for Flipkart) and 84% intend to continue using it (vs. 69%). ANOVA confirmed a statistically significant inter-platform satisfaction difference (F(1, 298) = 18.43, p < .001), and regression analysis revealed that consumer satisfaction significantly predicts loyalty intentions (β = 0.62, p < .001, R² = .38). Satisfaction differences are driven by platformlevel service quality differentials, particularly in delivery reliability and customer responsiveness. The study proposes strategic recommendations for both platforms to improve retention and competitive positioning in the Indian online retail market.

title: AIOS: A CPU-Native Inference Architecture for Large Language Models

detail.title: AIOS: A CPU-Native Inference Architecture for Large Language Models
detail.abstract: We present AIOS-a runtime architecture and model co-design framework for deploying large language models efficiently on CPU hardware. Current LLM inference engines were designed for GPU memory architecture and treat CPU as a fallback. We argue this is a design constraint, not a physics constraint, and that a first-principles approach to CPU memory hierarchy can achieve 50-92% reduction in DRAM data movement per generated token depending on model compliance with a proposed Model Contract. We decompose the inference bandwidth problem into four independent resource dimensions: weight reads, KV cache reads, activation memory spill, and attention compute. We propose five architectural requirements-the AIOS Model Contract-that models can be designed or fine-tuned to satisfy, and define four compliance tiers with corresponding performance projections. We present Mistral 7B as a baseline analysis [A] and Falcon 7B relufied as a reference implementation [P][V:#1], analytically projecting 80-85% MB/token reduction under full AIOS optimization [V:#2]. All quantitative projections are labeled by validation status. Empirical validation is tracked publicly on GitHub. AIOS is fully open source under Apache 2.0.

detail.title: Online Supplement: Effects of In-house and Wire Content Mix on Online Newspaper Subscriptions
detail.abstract: Declining circulation and advertising revenue have led many newspapers to cut costs by reducing in-house staff and relying more on wire content. In-house production provides unique content, while wire (non-exclusive) content offers broad coverage at lower cost. Using data from a regional U.S. newspaper, we examine how the mix of in-house and wire content affects subscription decisions. To address reader-side selection bias, we use local precipitation as an excluded variable to indirectly randomize readers’ exposure to content mix. We find that a 1% increase in the share of in-house articles raises daily subscriptions by 0.024% (≈9% of baseline) and by another 0.009% (≈4% of baseline) under a paywall. Against this overall trend, wire Business and Sports articles also increase conversion, suggesting opportunities for selective sourcing. Effects are weaker for local readers and for visitors from social media. Finally, readers from aggregators respond to in-house content and paywalls much like direct visitors, indicating that differentiation and paywalls remain effective even as readers turn to aggregators to discover news.

title: Will it Click? Advertising Strategy with Generative AI
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School, University of Cambridge - Judge Business School and Harvard Business School - Marketing Unit

detail.title: Will it Click? Advertising Strategy with Generative AI
detail.abstract: Increasingly, marketers are leveraging AI technologies to more effectively interact with consumers. In particular, many companies have adopted recent commercially available Generative AI (GenAI) capabilities (e.g., Open AI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini), which allow creating personalized messages at scale. In this paper, we model the impact of GenAI on advertising strategy. Firms seek to sell a product to consumers and can imperfectly identify their heterogeneous message preferences, i.e., which creative is most likely to prompt a response (or click). The firm has a baseline advertising message template and can use GenAI to adapt it and tailor a message to each consumer. However, GenAI-produced messages may deviate from the intended consumer's preference. In a monopoly setting, we find that the optimal advertising strategy will result in a click probability that exhibits an inverted U shape, depending on the consumer's message preference location along a Salop circle. We also uncover an interplay between the ability to identify consumers' preference locations and the GenAI technology. Specifically, if the GenAI technology is not too accurate, the optimal size of the segment the firm targets can be initially decreasing (i.e., advertising to fewer consumers) as the ability to identify consumers improves. The model is expanded to analyze the interaction between two competing firms armed with GenAI capabilities. We find that if a consumer is located closer to (farther from) a firm in the message space, counterintuitively, the probability of clicking on the firm's ad will decrease (increase) as GenAI's accuracy improves. As a result, better GenAI capability intensifies competition and leads to reduced profits; while the reverse is true as the ability to identify consumer preferences improves. We further endogenize GenAI capability and find that firms' investments in this technology form strategic substitutes, giving rise to an asymmetric equilibrium in which one firm invests more in GenAI capability than its rival. Lastly, when a firm can also identify heterogeneous consumer preferences in the product space, we find that prices tend to rise, as the firm can concentrate on higher willingness to pay consumers. However, for a given accuracy of product preference identification, improvements in GenAI capability may prompt a firm to reduce price, as it becomes advantageous to expand advertising reach and thus try to convert more price sensitive consumers. The findings have important managerial implications for firms as they seek to benefit from GenAI technologies, and provide guidance on how to formulate advertising strategies when employing them.

title: Constructive Falsity, Legal Truth, and The Public Interest in Not Reporting on Expunged Records

detail.title: Constructive Falsity, Legal Truth, and The Public Interest in Not Reporting on Expunged Records
detail.abstract: This Essay explores the tension between expungement law and the continued online publication of truthful news stories about arrests and criminal charges that have since been sealed or erased. Although constitutional doctrine and tort law largely foreclose remedies against publishers, the Essay revisits the normative assumptions underlying the existing legal framework. It first suggests that the concept of "public interest" in First Amendment jurisprudence is too broadly applied in the context of expunged records. It then considers whether the categorical rejection of "constructive falsity" fully accounts for the legal transformation expungement represents. Particularly, by applying the distinction between factual and legal truth to expungement laws, the Essay opens space for exploring intermediate approaches-such as declaratory remedies-that might better align expungement's rehabilitative aims with the functional permanence of digital information.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a medical embodiment study of the Mena Dominance Law (MDL) in critical care mortality modeling. The manuscript is intentionally narrower than the general MDL theory papers: it does not restate the law as a new universal claim, but evaluates whether MDL-derived representations carry clinically useful signal in intensive care unit (ICU) outcome prediction. The embodiment is studied across three major ICU resources-eICU, HiRID, and MIMIC-IV-together with cancer-focused subcohorts. The principal benchmark is SOFA, with emphasis on whether MDL-derived models, alone or in combination with SOFA, improve discrimination. Across the main strict six-organ cohorts, the combined MDL+SOFA models outperform SOFA-only models in every dataset. In eICU, strict six-organ AUC improves from 0.7533 for SOFA-only to 0.7954 for MDL-only and 0.8120 for MDL+SOFA. In HiRID, the corresponding values are 0.7759, 0.7805, and 0.8062. In MIMIC-IV, they are 0.6912, 0.7393, and 0.7562. Cancer subset analyses generally preserve the same directional pattern, although inference weakens materially in the smallest subgroup, the HiRID hematologic cancer-proxy strict organ-complete cohort. Beyond aggregate performance, the medical embodiment reveals structure that a pure summed severity score does not directly expose. Across datasets, non-survivors show both an upward shift in deficit burden and a redistribution of dominant-organ identity. In HiRID, survivors are most often respiratory-dominant, whereas deaths show relatively greater concentration in central nervous system, renal, and liver dominance. In MIMIC-IV, deaths are markedly more cardiovascular-dominant than survivors. These findings support the view that the embodiment captures structured multiorgan deterioration rather than undifferentiated severity alone. The strongest claim supported by the results is practical: in the declared critical-care embodiment studied here, MDL-derived features add clinically meaningful predictive information beyond SOFA and provide a more structured view of deficit organization across organ systems.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether education moderates the association between internet health information seeking and influenza vaccination, and whether this moderation changed after COVID-19. Using six waves of the National Health Interview Survey (2016-2018, 2022-2024; N > 150,000 adults, > 35,000 children), we find that education universally moderates the internet-vaccination association, but the moderation differs between adults and children. For adults, internet use is positively associated with vaccination across all education groups, but the association is significantly weaker for less-educated adults (HS total OR = 1.07 vs. bachelor's/master's+ OR = 1.36). For children, the moderation is qualitatively stronger: internet use is positively associated with vaccination among children of highly educated parents but not among children of less-educated parents. This gradient from quantitative to qualitative moderation is consistent with the Elaboration Likelihood Model prediction that educationbased differences in information processing ability are amplified in emotionally charged parental decision contexts. Four complementary trend specifications find no significant evidence that this moderation has changed over time, though confidence intervals are wide enough to include policy-relevant shifts. The education-vaccination gap is widening independently of internet use. Policy should prioritize building digital health literacy to extend the positive internet-vaccination association across education groups.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Boston University Questrom School of Business Research Paper (forthcoming)

detail.abstract: This paper studies how direct AI adoption, rather than AI skill hiring alone, reshapes firm-level labor demand. We construct a novel measure of operational AI adoption from 10-K filings using natural language processing, large language models, and a neural-network classifier, combine it with Webb's (2019) occupation-level AI exposure score, and link it to Lightcast job postings for Compustat firms from 2010 to 2022. Using a long difference design over one to five year horizons, we find that job postings in high exposure occupations decline over time following AI adoption, reaching -0.14 percent at the two-year horizon and -0.30 percent at the five-year horizon, with the richer specification reaching -0.32 percent at five years. Low-exposure occupations remain close to zero throughout. A falsification test confirms such a pattern is specific to operational AI deployment rather than broader AI engagement.  Heterogeneity analysis shows that the negative hiring response is concentrated in non-IT firms, is substantially stronger in manufacturing than in services, and is more pronounced among firms that adopt externally developed AI than among firms that build AI in-house. We also find that AI adoption is positively associated with labor productivity in the full sample and in both large and small firms. Taken together, the results suggest that AI adoption raises efficiency while selectively reducing demand in the occupations most exposed to automation. The paper contributes a new text-based measure of operational AI adoption, distinguishes buy versus build pathways, and documents heterogeneity in labor-demand adjustment across occupations and firm types.

title: Litigation Paper: When AI-Assisted Decisions Reach Litigation, What Evidence Actually Exists?
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Litigation Paper: When AI-Assisted Decisions Reach Litigation, What Evidence Actually Exists?
detail.abstract:
This paper argues that the primary litigation risk in enterprise AI is not merely model error, but evidentiary failure under scrutiny. When AI-assisted decisions are challenged, the decisive weakness may not be the output itself, but the institution’s inability to produce a contemporaneous, independently defensible record of what was relied upon, what was verified, who approved the consequential step and why that approval should survive hostile examination.

The paper develops this claim through the KEV framework and its central architectural constraint, V = 0: verification is absent at the point of generation. In legal terms, that means the output cannot serve as its own proof. If a consequential AI-assisted decision is later contested, the evidentiary substitute must already have been built elsewhere – in the organisation’s approval architecture, record design and evidentiary discipline. If it was not, governance language, policy artefacts and general model validation may do little to protect the institution once scrutiny becomes adversarial.

The analysis proceeds from an emerging design-accountability bridge into AI-assisted decisions, then explains V = 0 in legal terms, maps what scrutiny will actually demand and shows where the decision record disappears in practice. It examines the collapse of common governance language under examination, the distribution of liability across the decision chain, the insufficiency of vendor warnings as disclosure and the widening exposure created when content protection is mistaken for control preservation. It then sets out P = 1 as a minimum litigation-readiness threshold: before approval, can the organisation produce a contemporaneous, reconstructable decision pack that allows the decision to be defended without relying on the system’s own narrative?

The paper does not argue against AI use. It argues that where verification is absent at the generating act, accountability must be built elsewhere with enough discipline to survive challenge. Without that discipline, institutions may still obtain speed, convenience and commercial benefit. What they do not obtain is defensibility.

Technical Note Four established that VLI requires four calibrated inputs: direct deployment costs, mandatory verification overhead, failure-event cost and failure propagation probability. This annex tests how far those inputs can be calibrated from the public evidence alone.

The evidence base is uneven.  is the strongest variable because public cases already provide documented financial and institutional consequences across multiple sectors.  is weaker: public testing can show that error and hallucination remain materially present, and public litigation can show that propagation can be extreme under institutional reliance, but propagation remains governance-conditioned rather than universally measurable.  is the weakest variable in public accounting terms because organisations rarely disclose verification overhead separately, though public survey evidence shows that human validation and operating-model discipline remain material to successful AI deployment.  should usually be taken from an institution’s own contracts and infrastructure records and operating data rather than inferred from public averages. 

The core claim is simple and practical. Public evidence is already strong enough to show that Tier 3 verification liability cannot honestly be priced as trivial, theoretical or self-correcting. title: The Problem of Bi-Modal Distributions in Comparative Social Policy

detail.title: The Problem of Bi-Modal Distributions in Comparative Social Policy
detail.abstract: Global comparisons and international comparisons of different subjects, in different fields, of social policy are in general, many times non-thematized, nonrealized, many times blatantly obvious and in the spotlight, plagued by the phenomenon of, as Esping-Andersen (2000) has called it, the problem of bimodal distributions. That is, in one part of the world, or for one or more welfare regimes or welfare state systems, certain elements and conditions, causes and outcomes, of social policy (or social development, which is always an integral part of social policy analysis) are super relevant, and for most others, or all others, they simply are not. Soft economy jobs for women are a factual (existent) important feature of the welfare state (i.e. employment in public sector in mostly local governmentcontrolled enterprises/offices/service provision, e.g. railway and bus corporations, hospitals, social service organizations, government administrations, or government-owned electricity and other infrastructure-related companies and organizations, etc.), but they are not in most parts of the world, not in Latin America, Africa and Asia, as a matter of fact. The same is true of much-debated principles of e.g. decommodification, which only focuses on formal labor markets, excluding most situations and conditions of women, sexual minorities, ethnic minorities, rising scores of immigrant or transnational populations, as well as of course the majority of countries and populations in the world that preliminary work in the informal sector or simply worry about how to get clean water (not subject to arsenic poisoning), food and sanitation for themselves and their family members.

title: Standard Axioms of the Forces of Human Coordination: A Quantum Economics Point of View

detail.title: Standard Axioms of the Forces of Human Coordination: A Quantum Economics Point of View
detail.abstract: Knowledge does not increase steadily, it comes in shifts (cf Kuhn, 1970a,b, 1977, 1978). Often breakthroughs have not led to shifts in knowledge and theory development/adaptation, or the paradigm changes they  demanded. Scientific knowledge is more of than not its own most vicious enemy—outdated knowledge is the worst enemy of new knowledge. Old theories, by their long-serving theorists, get (gain and maintain) permanent status and permanent powers, by way of occupying all access points (e.g. occupying reviewers’ positions in the now universally applied mechanisms of the main and exclusively acknowledged publication channels). One such case in point is old/mainstream neoclassical economics versus praxeology theory as developed by Ludwig von Mises (1940/1949), and his rejection of equilibrium economics and of utility as an untenable concept (unscientific concept) (cf Aspalter, 2025; Mises, 1978). Mises has revolutionized mainstream economics theory, but the revolution never came to be, never was allowed to unfold, roll out. Neoclassical economics of the middle-to-late 19th century still rules the heads of most current mainstream economics thinkers of today.

Most recently, impact of monumental proportions was caused by Thomas Piketty’s 2013/2014 publication Capital in the Twenty-First Century. History (ourstory) is most influential and most rich in terms of vital findings in theory-making, welfare state system analysis, policy analysis, and of course social/societal/scientific problem analysis.

title: Communicational Social Policy

detail.title: Communicational Social Policy
detail.abstract: This article introduces the field and methods of communicational social policy. The core of communicational social policy, an emerging sub-field of social policy, is aptly embodied in Hong Kong’s Advertisements for the Public Interest (APIs), as practiced by the Hong Kong government intensively, and for decades already (HK, 2023). Any government in times of information society and digital society needs to catch up with international developments in terms of social policy delivery and new social policy innovations. Advertisements in the Public Interest (APIs) are such a strong and consequential pathbreaking innovation. Not only can communicational social policies replace to significant levels traditional monetary social policy, and thus help prevent fiscal collapses of governments, but also increase the preventative influence of policymaking, which is, in any case, welfare- and well-being-enhancing (cf Aspalter, 2010, 2014, 2015, 2020, 2021; Midgley and Aspalter, 2017). Physical and mental health policies, for example, may rise to new heights in terms of people coverage, preventative life-cycle behavioral health policy and social policy. The applications in the field of behavioral and communicational (informational/educational) social policies are endless, and open to innovation and wholesome, more humane and easily financially viable solutions.

detail.abstract: Does privatization weaken the state's ability to enforce core policies? We argue that state control over economic life underpins coercive state capacity through two mechanisms: economic leverage over livelihoods and administrative legibility of the population. Privatization can erode both. We test this argument in China and develop a novel measure of coercive capacity: excess births inferred from individual birth histories that we construct with population census. This measure tracks the enforcement gap of birth control, Beijing's longstanding policy priority. Exploiting county-level differences in the timing of agricultural decollectivization, we find that it substantially increased excess births. The effect is attenuated where households retained economic ties to the state and is accompanied by increased birth underreporting in local police records, consistent with the leverage and legibility mechanisms. Additional analyses rule out interpretations based on fertility intentions and highlight state responses to coercive capacity erosion following the retreat from economic control.

title: One-Time Marginal Haircut Wealth Tax

detail.title: One-Time Marginal Haircut Wealth Tax
detail.abstract: It is already become commonplace to ask for haircut dept cuts for poor, so-called developing, countries. The idea of haircut taxes has similar thought roots. The poor should gain freedom and relief from financial burden. While the former is poised at not letting the poor (countries here) pay more to the rich (countries), the latter aims at halting taxes for the poor and near poor (people) and taxing the super-super-rich (people) instead. New is now the idea of only taxing the super-super-rich with a new marginal and one-time wealth tax. Marginal means only above a certain threshold will be taxed, anything below will not be taxed. One-time taxation means people only have to pay it once, i.e. once in a lifetime. This is a historical-wrongs-turned-into-good kind of tax that makes historical wrongs being neutralized ex post. To be clear, historical wrongs can only be unwronged completely with the use of a time machine, and thus this new marginal haircut taxation on the super-super-rich is only makeshift solution to fix historical wrongs. Also, current wrongs are being fixed with this new marginal haircut wealth tax, as the poor children of the world are being wronged by the systems of the countries they are born in and being raised up in. The super-super-rich with this haircut wealth tax will be taxed to become only super rich, the first 50 or 100 million e.g. Euros or US dollars per person will not be taxed, and the succeeding millions will get a haircut taxation of a high percentage, but only once in their lifetime. The tax will be put on past wealth, e.g. the beginning of the last fiscal year. People cannot run away or avoid this taxation, or alter their behavior and somehow reduce/avoid taxation, as tax is being based on passed wealth, and governments (like that of France e.g.) in the past have proven to be very effective in taxing their own (even former) citizens even they have left the country (and long thereafter) (KPMG, 2020). This one-time marginal wealth tax was first proposed by Christian Aspalter (2023) in his 'Ten Worlds of Welfare Capitalism' book, having seen the need to propose a fast, fully capable taxation to end world hunger, world poverty, and world miseries on an epic scale in a very limited amount of time, and with rather overlookable/easy administrative means.

detail.abstract: This paper sets out to discuss the new organizing concept of the human capital welfare state (a special type of a social investment welfare state). It starts with the beginning of new organizing principles for the welfare state of the last one or two decades, such as the Third Way in the United Kingdom and other salient advances in this direction. Then, the paper painstakingly constructs, while building on sociological theories of particularly Anthony Giddens, Ulrich Beck, Niklas Luhmann, and Pierre Bourdieu, a new theoretical console for welfare state theory and policy, that is, the human capital welfare state. The new organizing concept of societal human capital/capabilities, as advanced in this paper, includes three dimensions, individual human capabilities, social capabilities, and cultural capabilities. At last six guiding principles of the human capital (capabilities) welfare state are outlined in greater detail: (a) a focus on prevention, effectiveness, and sustainability; (b) a mutual beneficial relationship between welfare state and economy; (c) the defense and development of societal human capital on individual, family, community and societal level; (d) empowerment and activation of the weak and disadvantaged; (e) social inclusion and social integration; (f) "environmental social policy."

title: Quantum Social Policy and the Role of Praxeology in Social Policy Science

detail.title: Quantum Social Policy and the Role of Praxeology in Social Policy Science
detail.abstract: What is quantum? A unit, a smallest unit of everything. In order to understand everything, the wholeness of everything and every wholeness within parts and bits of everything, one needs to look at its constituent elements. Albert Einstein told us that whatever small unit we are looking at we always look at a wholeness of something, again (cf Popper, 2007). What are the units in e.g. economics? Not scarcity, not markets, not money, not values. As Ludwig von Mises (1940/1949) so wonderfully made it clear, it are human actions. And these unit human actions cannot be separated from human communications, i.e. from human thinking, human planning, human calculations and feelings. I would add human entanglements, as all human action has been forged and is subject, and yet brings forth, a multitude of human entanglements (Aspalter, 2024). What beholds for economics also beholds for social policy. It is all about human action, including their planning, their evaluations, expected consequences and effects, including all their rational and irrational reasoning, feelings, with all their ideas and ideologies. This involves and necessitates networks, discourse, and forms of media that enable and guide/control it all.

title: Method of Theory Building

detail.title: Method of Theory Building
detail.abstract: This book is written for the advanced scholar and advanced student of any social science, be it social policy or economics, or education science, the specialty of Elizabeth Steiner. It holds a universal truth, as it is a universal guide for universal practice of theory interpretation and application and, for those who dare (and can or need), theory building. Most readers of this book will be interested in what is the nature of theories, and the nature of theory application or interpretation, and hence, in the following, theory description and theory evaluation. Others again will, on top, be interested in the main principles of theory building, as a scientific method, which, since it is scientific, always has to be universal (cf also Midgley, 2002). Science is about knowledge, Steiner teaches us; knowledge that can be tested and that is not particular, but instead universally true, across space and time. That is, any theory must be applicable in all countries, in all corners of the world, and in any century, decade and year.

title: The End of Social Insurance

detail.title: The End of Social Insurance
detail.abstract: The world of social policy, the academic world of social policy, is marked by rigid thoughts and unquestioned dogma-like beliefs and convictions. Like, social insurance is (would be) the only way to do social security, without it we are (would be) lost. And so it is with asset-and means-tested social assistance systems that cement, exacerbate and spread poverty and not cure and not reduce it (against many centuries-old beliefs and convictions, ignoring empirical and theoretical knowledge that proofs otherwise). Are we lost, would we, if social insurance would stop to function (end functioning, meaning ending to serve its purpose in social policy and social development)? This question can only be answered if one understands principal other choices of social security provision, what they are, how the work. The whole fear and anxiety that comes with sticking and blindly subscribing to seemingly, and fully mistaken, almighty effects and powers of social insurance systems is based on lack of knowledge. This article gives hereto an introduction.

title: Systemic Social Problems

detail.title: Systemic Social Problems
detail.abstract: Any quick search on the internet or one's library catalogue can reveal that systemic social problems have not yet become mainstream, i.e. they are yet to be mainstreamed as a whole, the very most of them (cf Head, 2018). In social policy research, and social science research in general, the prevalent focus on handy choices of sealed and/or compartmentalized social problems (including economic and health problems, etc.) in the past is perhaps significantly responsible for the relative lack of higher-level systemic social problem analyses. Neither a great number of studies, nor strong or frequent research programs, on systemic social problems are visible in general social policy and social science literature. Yet, in recent years more and more studies are taking up the lead in this positive and utterly necessary direction. This is to a very large extent the outcome of media and public discourses on the subject, which once again supports the finding that social problems are identified and debated among four main actors. Either the media (including social media), the government, the experts (such as social policy scientists and practitioners) and the general public at large are pointing to, shaping and constantly reshaping social problem discourses. The same is true for systemic social problems, that either (a) talk about problems of social systems, like the economy, the education system, governance or administrative systems, or (b) talk about interrelated social problems (i.e. problem constellations of various complexity) and/or wicked problems (which require high analytical and/or remedial complexity). Both of which may require majorsystemic, paradigmatic-solutions or sets of solutions, including one or many systemic changes of all sorts. Not all wicked and/or interrelated problems are systemic problems, and not all systemic problems are wicked and/or interrelated problems. But they are to a very large extent present in the same problem or problem constellation at hand. Interrelated social problems (i.e. problem constellations) that are systemic, or wicked social problems that require systemic solutions, are yet largely under the radar or neglected in general theory making and in general social policy practice alike.

The Federal Reserve’s 2022-23 tightening cycle involved the use of two monetary policy tools: changes in administrative rates and changes in the size of its balance sheet. detail.abstract: Using home insurance policy-level data from 2009 to 2024, we study how premiums and coverage respond to properties' exposure to flood risk. title: From Techne Equalisation to Phronesis Premium: Generative AI and Seniority Bias in Ageing Europe

detail.title: From Techne Equalisation to Phronesis Premium: Generative AI and Seniority Bias in Ageing Europe
detail.abstract: Contrary to the prevailing view that older workers are disadvantaged by or unable to keep pace with technological change, this paper argues that generative AI may advantage them at the expense of younger ones. The mechanism operates through two channels. First, generative AI equalises procedural competence (techne) across occupations and within the same occupation and task, enabling average and lower-performing workers to reach the quality of top performers, an executional prosthesis that recovers skills depreciated with age. Second, as execution becomes cheap and replicable, the scarce factor shifts to skills that AI cannot easily replicate yet, such as contextual judgment and responsible decision-making (phronesis), capabilities that correlate with reflective experience and age rather than with technical currency. The seniority bias finds support in an empirical exercise on Eurostat EU-LFS data (2008-2025): the youth employment share in high-AI-adoption sectors diverges sharply downward after the diffusion of ChatGPT, following fifteen years of no statistically significant differential trend relative to the rest of the economy, while the senior share expands. In ageing Europe, this mechanism offers a partial response to demographic contraction. It carries, however, significant downsides, some inherent to the equalising effect itself (the devaluation of top performers, convergence toward good enough, the raising of the performance bar) and others to the revaluation of phronesis (the erosion of the training pipeline through which future judgment is formed). The advantage is transitory and self-undermining, depending on technological advancement, shifting social expectations, and the self-erosion of the very conditions that sustain it; in addition, its scope is shaped by the design choices of AI producers. The policy debate should focus on two questions: how to harness the benefits of the equalising effect and the recovery of phronesis while they last, while counteracting their adverse consequences, and how to preserve human relevance in AI-governed systems.

detail.title: Improving e-scooter safety through kinematic data-based event detection
detail.abstract: The growing popularity of e-scooters as a micro-mobility option has been accompanied by increased safety risks. Multiple studies highlight the impact of infrastructure on e-scooter riders during safety-critical events, emphasizing the need to identify locations where such incidents occur. However, from a preventive perspective on traffic safety, it is essential to identify these locations before an e-scooter crash occurs. This paper takes the first step towards this by proposing a novel methodology that utilizes machine learning and kinematic data from e-scooters. A comprehensive procedure is designed to prepare a labeled dataset from naturalistic e-scooter rides. Then, techniques for filtering sensor noise and extracting machine learning features are discussed. Finally, machine learning algorithms are trained and evaluated using appropriate performance metrics. Across multiple metrics, the ensemble models outperformed traditional classification algorithms, with XGBoost achieving the best overall performance. These validated models, when combined with GPS signals, can detect safety-critical events and then help identify locations associated with e-scooter infrastructure where such events occur.

detail.title: Learning How To Borrow in a Fintech World: Consumer Behavior When Search Costs Are (Near) Zero
detail.abstract: Online loan marketplaces are changing consumer lending. Here we investigate consumer behavior in these markets with near-zero search costs. Using administrative data on 730,000 applications, 750,000 offers, and 200,000 individuals, together with credit registry records, we document four facts. First, substantial within-applicant dispersion in offered terms makes search highly valuable. Second, marketplace nudges mitigate choice complexity. Third, applicants search significantly, applying repeatedly, asking for different terms, and rejecting offers, in ways consistent with their creditworthiness. Fourth, dynamic adverse selection constrains search, as lenders penalize repeat applicants. Our findings highlight trade-offs between informational gains from search, and reputational and cognitive costs.

detail.title: Managing Solar–Battery Use Under Uncertainty: Prosumer Risk Preferences Across Gains and Losses
detail.abstract: Power-system benefits from residential solar–battery systems are amplified when many households sell stored electricity to the grid during peak hours under centralized coordination. However, the revenues from such arrangements are inherently uncertain and evaluated differently when given as potential gains or avoided losses. To examine this type of decision-making, we conduct a split-sample discrete choice experiment (n=1,027), administering gain- and loss-domain surveys to Belgian subsamples that are representative by age, gender, and region. In each survey, respondents choose between guaranteed bill savings from self-consumption and probabilistic revenues from energy-selling agreements managed either by the household or an external actor. We observe two behavioral patterns that are central to cumulative prospect theory: overweighting of small probabilities and diminishing sensitivity to value changes relative to a reference point. This latter pattern is consistent with the reflection effect—risk aversion in gains and risk preference in losses—as reinforced by respondents being more likely to choose the guaranteed outcome when evaluating gains rather than losses. Beyond this gain–loss reference effect, our results show that households are more willing to enter energy-selling agreements when they can delegate dispatch decisions to established institutions such as energy retailers and system operators, rather than a private aggregator or self-management. Together, the observed diminishing sensitivity, probability weighting, and manager preferences—along with their variation across age and education profiles—reveal targeted and complementary policy levers. These include downside guarantees and incentive-compatible billing structures designed to reduce perceived risk and expand participation in coordinated energy-selling programs.

detail.abstract: Natural disasters often raise gasoline prices when they disrupt upstream fuel supply, but less is known about disasters that primarily disrupt local mobility and access. We examine the short-run effect of the 2024 Park Fire on retail gasoline prices in Northern California using high-frequency station-level data and a distance-based research design. Benchmark two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences estimates show that stations near the wildfire experienced price declines relative to more distant stations, with the largest effects concentrated within 10 miles of the fire perimeter. Because treated and control stations do not fully satisfy parallel pre-trends in the weekly panel, we use synthetic difference-in-differences as our preferred estimator. The SDID results confirm a negative local price response: gasoline prices fell by 2.5 cents per gallon for stations within 20 miles of the wildfire and by 3.9 cents for stations within 10 miles during the six weeks following fire onset. The effect attenuates as the post-treatment window expands and is concentrated among rural and unbranded stations. Taken together, the spatial, temporal, and heterogeneity patterns are more consistent with a localized contraction in gasoline demand than with a broad supply-driven fuel shock. More broadly, the results show that disaster-induced gasoline price responses depend on the dominant channel of disruption and are not uniformly upward.

detail.title: Housing Costs and Fertility: Evidence from Nonlinear Affordability Thresholds
detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the relationship between housing costs and fertility by addressing measurement bias and nonlinear effects in housing affordability. Standard rent-to-income measures may be mechanically endogenous, as childbirth can reduce household income and inflate affordability ratios. To overcome this issue, we measure housing costs using monthly rent levels. Using approximately 1.8 million renter observations from the American Community Survey, we estimate a threshold model to assess whether the effect of housing costs varies across affordability regimes. We identify a statistically significant rent threshold that separates two distinct regimes. Below the threshold, increases in rent are associated with economically meaningful reductions in the probability of childbirth. Above the threshold, the marginal effect becomes small and statistically indistinguishable from zero. To address potential endogeneity in housing costs, we exploit exogenous variation in local rents and find consistent evidence of this nonlinear pattern. Additional analyses show that the threshold effect is strongest among women aged 30-34, corresponding to peak childbearing years. These findings indicate that housing affordability constraints operate primarily within specific cost ranges rather than uniformly across the rent distribution. More broadly, the results highlight the importance of measurement and functional form in identifying demographic responses to housing market conditions

detail.title: Fixed capital, labor, and carbon footprint: A redefinition of consumer responsibility
detail.abstract: Accurate attribution of carbon emission responsibility is a prerequisite for effective global climate governance. To improve responsibility attribution, we develop an end-use environmentally extended input-output (EEIO) model that closes fixed capital and labor. The model captures emission flows overlooked in the conventional EEIO models. Specifically, it represents the circular process in which emissions embodied in fixed capital stocks and labor re-enter the production process through consumption of fixed capital and labor input. Applying this model to 164 countries and regions from 2000 to 2018, we demonstrate that it corrects systematic biases, raising high-income countries’ carbon footprints while lowering those of others. For instance, while the EEIO carbon footprint gap between China (11.42 Gt) and the United States (6.29 Gt) was large, the end-use EEIO model reveals a much narrower disparity (6.02 Gt vs 6.22 Gt). Structural Decomposition Analysis identifies the final demand scale effect as the dominant driver of global carbon footprint growth, whereas the declining carbon intensities of industries, fixed capital, and labor act as the primary mitigating forces. Moreover, the reassessment of decoupling reveals that the conventional EEIO model has overstated the progress of green transitions, particularly in developed countries. The end-use EEIO model yields a global CO₂-GDP elasticity of 0.39 compared with the conventional model’s 0.42. These findings highlight that incorporating carbon emissions embodied in fixed capital and labor in carbon footprint accounting is critical for accurate responsibility attribution and sustainable development.​

detail.abstract: The Trump Administration and U.S. Congress are promoting new ventures to extract valuable minerals from outer space. This Article does not dismiss the idea out of hand, but explores reasons for caution, including practical problems with space mining, its environmental impact, the likelihood that the United States could violate international law, and the risk of armed conflict. These problems are exacerbated by financial conflicts of interest in our government with a handful of billionaires, who have a financial interest in space mining work. Space mining, if it becomes economically feasible, may be inevitable, and this means that it is important to work toward multinational agreements to regulate it rather than assume that enforceable principles of international law will prohibit it.

detail.title: Cross-Border Spillover Effects of Marijuana Dispensaries on Child Protective Services
detail.abstract: I estimate the cross-border spillover effects of legalized recreational marijuana dispensaries on child protective services (CPS) reporting in a neighboring prohibition state. While existing research focuses on effects within legalizing states, little is known about impacts on neighboring prohibition states. Exploiting spatial and temporal variation in proximity to dispensaries in Wisconsin following legalization in neighboring Michigan and Illinois, I estimate that a 100-mile reduction in distance increases CPS report rates by 7 percent for children under age 13. Effects are concentrated among reports from non-mandated reporters, children with prior CPS involvement, and neglect allegations. The findings highlight the importance of interstate coordination in drug policy, clear CPS screening guidance, and supportive services for families affected by substance use.

detail.title: Tariffs in a Multi-Player Economy
detail.abstract: This Article argues that tariffs cannot be understood through border mechanics or political slogans alone. In a multi-player economy, tariffs operate through interconnected supply chains, pricing structures, strategic dependencies, and allied relationships, which means their effects rarely remain confined to the intended foreign target. The familiar claim that "they pay" therefore obscures the more difficult question of economic incidence, which often falls substantially on domestic importers, firms, and consumers. More broadly, the Article contends that tariff policy cannot be evaluated in the abstract. Whether a tariff is defensible depends on the objective being pursued, whether revenue, coercion, resilience, or industrial adjustment, and on a candid account of burdens, time horizon, strategic sectors, and allied spillovers. The Article concludes by proposing a disciplined framework for evaluating tariff policy as strategy rather than political posture.

The developments have been described and their effects on societal change explained. The paper also in all briefness addresses the main response that social policy could potentially come up with.

Whereas both countries will suffer severely from ageing of society, China in addition also has to cope with fast changing economic transition and its accompanying social changes, particularly domestic migration and modernization of society.

title: Third Modernity and Social Policy

detail.title: Third Modernity and Social Policy
detail.abstract: This paper identifies the onset of "Third Modernity" with the coming of artificial intelligence and its applications, as well as enhanced digitalization, back in the year 2016. This article emphasizes its effects on human employment, which are truly devastating in the years and decades to come. The social policy solutions to the multiple conundrums of artificial intelligence, societal aging and climate change are to be fundamental and systemic in nature. Building on decades of normative social policy research, this article puts forward three new fundamental social policy strategies that focus on (i) incentive mechanisms in social security and social assistance provision, (ii) health education and early diagnosis, as well as (iii) 'smart' targeted universal benefits and services. And in addition to that, the author predicts the coming of universal basic income schemes, in numerous developed and fast developing societies alike.

title: Towards 'Human Capital Solidarity': Emphasizing Justice in the Distribution of Physical, Mental, Social and Cultural Capabilities - A Normative Study in Social Policy

detail.abstract: The last couple of decades have seen a succession of new paradigms in social policy, particularly social security policy. Pension and health care systems have seen major, and many times systematic, changes on average every couple of years. This paper aims to introduce a new perspective to social policy that has not been pursued so far - that is, delivering social solidarity by focusing on human resources (i.e. physical, mental, social and cultural capabilities) developing the human capital solidarity approach. The human capital solidarity approach focuses on long-term lifetime perspectives and the need to achieve short-term goals; it focuses also on mental and environmental sides of social problems, rather than trying to fix every problem with a monetary solution alone. The new approach also introduces new concepts of e.g. ‘environmental social policy’, ‘cultural social policy’, and ‘social policy marketing’.

title: The Field-to-Hospital Data Gap in Disaster Response: A Persistent Failure Point in Continuity of Care and the Case for an NFC-Based Offline Patient Tracker

detail.title: The Field-to-Hospital Data Gap in Disaster Response: A Persistent Failure Point in Continuity of Care and the Case for an NFC-Based Offline Patient Tracker

detail.abstract: In mass casualty events and large-scale emergencies, clinical data gathered by field providers is routinely lost before it reaches the receiving facility. Triage classification, medication administration, vital sign trends, and mechanism of injury are established at the point of first contact and transmitted verbally at handoff, if at all. Receiving teams restart without that context, repeating assessments and making treatment decisions from zero. This failure is not a product of inadequate effort or protocol adherence; it reflects structural limitations in how clinical information is captured, carried, and retained under austere conditions. Existing approaches each break down in predictable ways when infrastructure fails: networked records require connectivity that disasters destroy; paper tags degrade and detach during transport; verbal handoff produces significant information loss even under routine conditions. This paper examines the field-to-hospital data gap and the case for a patient-carried, infrastructureindependent approach to closing it. Near Field Communication (NFC) technology provides a practical mechanism: passive, battery-free tags that store structured clinical records and transmit them to any NFC-enabled smartphone without network connectivity, institutional login, or interoperability between agency systems. Attached to a patient at first clinical contact, an NFC tag carries a complete record through every subsequent handoff, readable at the receiving facility regardless of infrastructure status. The paper reviews the evidence on handoff-related patient harm, analyses the limitations of current documentation approaches in disaster settings, and makes the case for a controlled pilot study to validate NFC-based offline patient tracking in mass casualty environments. Collaboration with academic and operational partners is the necessary next step toward establishing the clinical evidence base for this approach.

title: Digital Health Technologies and Certified Nursing Assistants in Long-Term Care: A Scoping Review of Adoption, Barriers, and Impact on Care Quality

detail.title: Digital Health Technologies and Certified Nursing Assistants in Long-Term Care: A Scoping Review of Adoption, Barriers, and Impact on Care Quality

detail.abstract:
Background: Certified nursing assistants (CNAs) represent the largest segment of direct-care staff in long-term care (LTC) facilities, providing approximately 80% to 90% of hands-on care to nursing home residents. Despite their central role, CNAs remain largely absent from digital health technology (DHT) research compared to registered nurses and physicians. This scoping review, the first to specifically examine the intersection of DHTs and the CNA workforce in LTC, aimed to map and synthesize the existing literature on DHT adoption, barriers, facilitators, and impact on care quality among CNAs.

Methods: The review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines and the five-stage framework proposed by Arksey and O'Malley. A systematic search was performed across four databases—PubMed, Google Scholar, CINAHL, and Scopus—for studies published between January 2015 and March 2026 that addressed CNAs or equivalent direct-care workers using any form of DHT in LTC settings. Citation tracking supplemented the database searches. Out of 542 initially identified records, 187 duplicates were removed, 355 records were screened by title and abstract, 305 were excluded, and 50 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility. Twenty-four studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final qualitative synthesis.

Results: Findings were organized into four thematic areas: (a) types of digital health technologies used by CNAs, with electronic health records being the most frequently studied specific technology (n = 5), followed by AI/machine learning (n = 4) and robotic systems (n = 2); eight studies examined multiple technology types; (b) barriers to technology adoption, including limited digital literacy, inadequate training programs (often 30 minutes or less), cost constraints, and the systematic exclusion of CNAs from technology design and implementation decisions; (c) facilitators of technology adoption, including perceived usefulness, hands-on training with peer mentoring, strong management support, and user-centered design that incorporates CNA input; and (d) impact on care quality, where evidence remained limited and mixed, with some studies reporting improved documentation accuracy and communication efficiency, though few directly measured resident health outcomes such as falls, pressure ulcers, or hospitalization rates. The majority of included studies (n = 20) were published after 2020, and although four studies examined AI technologies, none specifically addressed artificial intelligence in direct relation to CNA practice.

Conclusion: This review reveals a critical evidence gap and underscores the urgent need for CNA-inclusive research designs, dedicated technology training programs tailored to the unique needs of frontline direct-care workers, and policy reforms that address structural inequities in technology access. As long-term care demand intensifies amid rapid technological advancement, ensuring that CNAs are empowered, supported, and meaningfully integrated into health care's digital evolution is both a workforce imperative and a fundamental issue of care quality and health equity.

title: Normativity and Its Two Main Different Streams

detail.title: Normativity and Its Two Main Different Streams
detail.abstract: This article focuses on the existence of two main interpretations of normativity, i.e. what is meant by normativity in social policy, explaining their difference and hence help ensure theoretical and practical clarity. The word normative is used and (hence) thought to stand for many different things for different sciences, and for different scientists. But, in social policy, the term normative social policy should mean evaluative and/or prescriptive social policy (Pinker, 1971; Durkheim, 1928). There are different traditions and within each different streams of normative social policy theories and conceptual models. The two most fundamentally diverse groupings, or traditions, one can distinguish are, first, a philosophical tradition of normativity and, second, a pragmatic/professional consulting-oriented tradition of normative thinking and theories; in short normativity in general.

title: Lessons for Health Care Policy in the United States: Comparing Health Care Systems

detail.title: Lessons for Health Care Policy in the United States: Comparing Health Care Systems
detail.abstract: This paper compares health care systems. It looks beyond normal academic, political, or journalistic rhetoric, by exactly sticking to facts, i.e. empirical data (in particular data provided by the WHO) and comprehensive case study analyses. The paper finds that a number of myths and common believes in health care policy are not supported by emprical evidence. Global health care policy, as well as health care policy in United States, needs to look at statistical data and profound overall assessment studies to change global health care policies. The paper reveals that there is ample room for saving costs, i.e. increase efficiency, of public health care systems in order to save lives. Good health care and more health care can be generated by 'administrative' and 'incentive' reforms (usually involving systemic and structural reforms) of health care systems. Many millions of lives can be saved if we stick to statistical empricial data and case studies, and distance ourselves from harmful ideological blindness in health care politics.

title: Political Will and Social Policy

detail.title: Political Will and Social Policy
detail.abstract: There is no definition that fits, one that captures really what 'political will' is (cf Post and Raile, 2010; Marquette, 2020). It is a conundrum indeed, for social scientists in the political arena, it is and must be one of the greatest, if not the greatest, impediment (mystery, problem, issues, pick any one description you like). It, for me, it seems naturally the same problem as the coordination problem of Friedrich Hayek (1945, 1937, 1933). Not only is it analogous, no, it is the very same unidentified, unexplained, unsolved giant, in the theoretical castle in mainstream economics and mainstream politics alike. Collective planning/action (by all market players, by all members of society) on the one side and political will of the government, of the elites, the experts, and rank and file government officers and administrators on the other. They are obviously not the same thing, but they are explained by the same kind of forces, both of them are. For those who have had a chance, and opted for it, and pulled it through, to read my recent book on Human Entanglement Theory (2024a) or the earlier article on the same subject, on Human Quantum Mechanics (2024b), may already know what comes next.

title: Defensive Trademark Registration: Benefits, Legal Risks, And The Position Of The Law
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Defensive Trademark Registration: Benefits, Legal Risks, And The Position Of The Law
detail.abstract:
In the world of intellectual property, trademarks are more than just symbols or logos; they are the lifeblood of a brand's identity and reputation. They serve as distinctive signposts that identify the source of goods or services and enable consumers to distinguish one enterprise from another in the marketplace. By securing exclusive rights in a mark, trademark helps businesses to protect their brand image, preserve their goodwill, and prevent unauthorised use that may cause confusion among consumers or dilute the value of their brand.[1] Trademarks have also become critical strategic assets in global commerce, particularly for companies seeking to expand internationally, and are increasingly recognised as key drivers of intangible value.

Therefore, in response to the growing commercial value of trademarks, some businesses employ a proactive strategy known as defensive trademark to further safeguard their intellectual property. This involves registering trademarks in multiple classes of goods or services, including those in which the proprietor may not have immediate commercial operations, with the aim of preventing competitors from registering identical or similar marks and exploiting the brand’s reputation.[2] While defensive trademark registration can offer valuable protection and strategic advantages, it also presents legal, financial, and regulatory challenges, particularly in jurisdictions where trademark rights are tied to bona fide use. In this article, the advantages and disadvantages of defensive trademark registration, as well as the legal position on this practice, are critically examined.

title: Thought Experiments in Social Policy Analysis

detail.title: Thought Experiments in Social Policy Analysis
detail.abstract: They serve different purposes and are of different kinds. Thought experiments, by and large, are a technique within theory building, theory promoting and/or theory debating. A great deal of unimaginable, previously unthought (by most), hard to understand, and unknowingly and/or stubbornly wrongly understood (by and large) conclusions are the goal of thought experiments. Sometimes the intended audience of thought experiments are the researchers/theory builders themselves, often the general scientific and/or public audience is targeted. The history of thought experiments is probably as old as imagination, religion, stories told, actions planned and simply profound, complex and comprehensive thoughts are spun.

title: The Underbelly of Science: Caught Between Untenability and Meaninglessness

detail.title: The Underbelly of Science: Caught Between Untenability and Meaninglessness
detail.abstract: Most people never care, most people never get to care. They do not read those papers, they do not open those books. Science if full of them, in fact, John Ioannidis (2005) proclaimed in some parts of the science park they make up the majority of studies out there that run under the banner of science, that claim, pretend or the very most just imitate science (cf also Ioannidis, 2014, 2021, 2024; Ioannidis et al., 2017). Let's do aside with name calling, let's not fall into the Popperian fallacy of calling names, of science and non-science (Popper, 1959, 2007, 2009). There are though different degrees of qualities of scientific studies conducted, ranging from zero quality (zero truth, zero excellence) to maximum quality (maximum truth, maximum excellence). Mises (1940/1949) famously called these zero, to not close to any meaningful or not close to any acceptable, quality studies and publications, their theories and findings, "untenable". A very polite, and sophisticated nevertheless, phrasing of the problem: untenable. This means it cannot be held up, it needs to be disregarded, discarded (into the bin that usually stands in the corner of one's office). In general it is really difficult, I think (i.e. with a high probability, but far from certain) for all of us, or at least the very most of us, to come up with meaningful research goals plus meaningful research methods, and yet also meaningful research findings all the time, or again and again. But, this is the beauty of science, not all is given, one has to put in effort, sometimes decades of efforts, sometimes (many times) things are in vain, for good reason, science is hard, science is supposed to be really meaningful, and it is really hard to be really meaningful, for most research fields, topics, and chosen research problems, given the lack of data, or experiments, the lack of full theoretical (e.g. causal) understanding, lack of time and money, and so forth. For science to be entering the field of meaningfulness, and at the same time leaving the field of untenability, it needs to fulfill (follow) key imperatives.

title: Nudging Is Bullying

detail.title: Nudging Is Bullying
detail.abstract: The new hype of nudging in public policy and economics needs to come to an end. Nudging, in terms of outcomes (not intentions) is bullying! This is unethical to the core, and scientists and practitionners are already changing their attitudes. Buzzwords, and buzz concepts, are dangerous, when accepted unchecked!

title: The Interplay between Different Streams of Social Policy Theory

detail.title: The Interplay between Different Streams of Social Policy Theory
detail.abstract: A very good description of the problems of the interplay between different streams of social policy theory is given by Modood and Favell (2003), as well as Bauböck (2008). They discussed the key problems that arise from e.g., as in a (shockingly) large number of cases, working on social policy description (case studies, thematic papers, historical/ourstorical papers, etc.) and casually adding normative lessons or suggestions. Or conducting blindly descriptive social policy research projects or research works without knowing (as in most cases, as there are barely social policy-own normative theories), or not understanding normative social policy theory (having not fully read them, as so often, or simply not having gotten the gist of things, or not yet). Also, running evaluations and prescriptions (normativity-based social policy research projects and research studies) without fully knowing the empirical reality on the ground, is a monster-sized problem in social policy science, as most studies and books concentrate only on a very small number of countries (and that among Western countries). Global multicenter case studies are yet super seldom, and they themselves represent a very good starting point in analyzing and conquering (intellectually, and scientifically that is) the whole world-with all the people in it, in all countries, in all corners (on all plains, in all valleys, on all mountains, on all islands)-within the realm and discipline of social policy. Medical science and the field of health policy is a head of social policy science in applying multicenter social policy analyses. If one looks for it there are a larger number of multicenter case studies in social policy, but they are only a tiny fraction of all case studies, and yet not fully noticed, with their great value not yet fully appreciated far and wide. The great usefulness of such studies is shown e.g. by Wong and Ho (2023) when analyzing the impact and response measures to the Covid-19 Pandemic in several cities around the world, going both deep and wide, as is the winning formula of multicenter case study analysis. Quantitative global local data analysis is the next step up after ordinary global data analysis. In abolishing the container view of looking at nation states, we in social policy science in particular need to focus on (global) local data, not on national-aggregated, averaged(!)-data. Schumpeter (1951) knew about the problems of science based on (scientifically random, meaningless, fully obscuring) national boundaries and their aggregates. Social policy science needs to follow this imperative.

detail.abstract: The study investigates the equilibrium relationships and dynamic causal interactions among economic growth, energy generation, energy consumption, and carbon emissions in Papua New Guinea, using annual time-series data from 2000 to 2024. The objective is to assess the presence of energy-led growth in GDP, both in the short-run and long-run. The stationarity of the variables was tested using the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) unit root tests, followed by Johansen's cointegration tests to identify long-term relationships. A Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) was employed to capture short-run dynamics, with Granger causality tests and Impulse Response Functions (IRFs) used to analyze directional influence and temporal responses. The results reveal cointegration among the series, indicating stable long-term relationships. In the short-run, both energy generation and energy consumption granger-cause GDP, suggesting a unidirectional energy-led growth pattern. IRFs show that a unit shock in either energy variable induces modest, fluctuating responses in GDP that dissipate over time, converging toward equilibrium in the long-run. These findings underscore the strategic importance of energy sector development in driving economic growth, while highlighting the need for sustainable energy policies to balance growth objectives with environmental considerations.

detail.abstract: Repo markets clear either bilaterally over the counter (OTC) or through central counterparties (CCPs), which differ in how counterparty risk is priced. In bilateral markets, repo rates reflect borrower-specific risk, while CCP clearing pools counterparties and applies a common pricing rule. We develop a model of security-driven repo in which repo rates are non-linear in borrower risk. As a result, averaging borrower-specific OTC prices yields more negative rates than pricing the pooled borrower in CCP markets. The model predicts that the CCP–OTC specialness gap compresses during periods of counterparty uncertainty and varies with borrower and collateral characteristics. Using transaction-level data from the euro-area interbank repo market around the March 2020 COVID-19 shock, we find evidence consistent with these predictions. Our results show that central clearing dampens specialness in normal times but stabilizes repo pricing during stress.

detail.abstract: This paper explains the crime scene investigation method in social policy analysis. Social policy as a science has a been subject to a great number of expanding realms of applications. Social policy as a science in the past has been constantly addressing—and needs to address—new problems, new aspects of human lives/governance/societies, and entire new fields of sciences that ask for solutions, for social policy solutions (from recent Covid-19 pandemic responses, health outcomes, and losses of human dignity, to ongoing climate change and its impact on human lives and human civilizations, and artificial intelligence making human work redundant and hence obsolete, and so forth). Topics and tasks at hand, or in front of us, on the road ahead (be it tomorrow, in two years from now, or decades and centuries down the road) have pushed, and are pushing, social policy to reveal its limits.

title: Spectral Data Analysis

detail.title: Spectral Data Analysis
detail.abstract: The development of discipline-specific methodology has been a forgotten child of social policy science. Yet, naturally social policy scientists focus a great deal on the power of case study analyses (Yin, 1994a,b), and mixed methods (Brannen, 1992, 2005, 2021). Some methods are overused, while others are underused, not used, and quite often simply not pointed out-the usage of methods is often automatically practiced, without developing the theory of methodology, and without pointing to the specific methods used, how they work, and/or their difference to other methods. In 2023, Aspalter, pointed out, explained and emphasized the understanding, rationale and usage of the spectral data analysis, comparing and differentiating it from other disciplines' usages, like famously in physics and chemistry, as well as economics. In physics, we look at e.g. black holes (and try to find white holes, and grey holes) when looking at the stars, with the right equipment of course. In chemistry, we look at tiniest (so it seems) things, also with the right equipment of course. While normal pictures are out of the question, scientists in both cases use a special technique, i.e. in physics they look at any kind of emissions, their distortions/diversions, and so forth; in chemistry e.g. they also look at emissions e.g. after radiating the object under investigation. As welfare state systems, in social policy science, do not produce, reflect or bend light, radio or gamma waves, or emit/reflect radiation, things are different. The flow of work steps is different, and the location and the nature of the object under scrutiny also differ entirely. In general, in the social sciences, the method of spectral data analysis can be defined as: "the determination of the constitution, conditions and/or functioning … of the research objects … by means of determining and analyzing spectra of distinct outcomes and patterns of outcomes they produce." (Aspalter, 2023a: 28)

title: Container Science, Container Social Policy
