Beck particularly fleshed out the idea of container sociology, where the compartmentalization into nation states that resemble arbitrary containers that determine what we look at and what we see and measure in science, be it in sociology or economics, or other sciences.

detail.abstract:
This Article argues that the appointment of prominent wellness and antivaccine figures to senior federal health positions marks the culmination of a long-running evolution in American health fraud—from nineteenth-century traveling medicine shows to the institutional capture of government health agencies. Drawing a direct lineage from patent medicine marketing to contemporary wellness conspiracism, this Article demonstrates how tactics perfected by early medicine show entrepreneurs—emotional manipulation, conspiratorial framing, anti-establishment positioning, and the exploitation of information asymmetries—have persisted across regulatory and technological shifts, ultimately achieving unprecedented political legitimacy.

 This Article traces this evolution through the deregulated supplement marketplace created by the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994, the amplification of health misinformation by social media platforms, and the COVID-19 pandemic’s destabilization of public trust in scientific authority. It then examines how these dynamics enabled the elevation of wellness-aligned figures to leadership roles at the Department of Health and Human Services, the National Institutes of Health, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and the Food and Drug Administration. The resulting transformation of federal health agencies—from evidence-based institutions into platforms for wellness ideology—has produced immediate public health consequences, including mass resignations of career officials, preventable disease outbreaks, and erosion of America’s scientific credibility.

 By situating contemporary wellness governance within a longer history of health fraud and regulatory arbitrage, this Article contends that the phenomenon of “government gone Goop” represents a broader crisis of democratic governance: whether institutions tasked with protecting the public can maintain epistemic integrity in information environments that reward confusion, distrust, and commercially profitable misinformation.

Developmental Social Policy is a normative (prescriptive) social policy theory that offers strategies and policy solutions to prevent and reduce any social problems, also health care problems, such as the high rates of mortality and sufferings caused by prominent modern mass diseases (or non-communicable diseases, NCDs) of our time. This study gives detailed, practical and realistic policy suggestions, based on a preventative health policy strategy, as is laid out by and supported by the theory of Developmental Social Policy.

title: Social Contracts as Power Relations

detail.title: Social Contracts as Power Relations
detail.abstract: To interpret history is nothing else than to reinterpret it, in one's own ways, where however one's own ways are never what they seem, one's own ways. Our thoughts are the music that one hears for oneself, but the instruments have been constructed, arranged and conducted, and played again and again, in the past by the whole of humanity, to be precise, the ones that control humanity and their vassals. Our actions, our measures, our senses, arguments and rationalizations are never new, they rose from the past, there are controlled from the past (Nietzsche, 1878, 1887), far distant past and the immediate past. In addition, the future also controls the present, by way of expectations and evaluations of future events and developments (especially expectations of repercussions or rewards of any kind). Social contracts are attempts to interpret/reinterpret our past, our human past, of civilization and modernization, in order to legitimize power today, and down the road into the future. Power relations are what made us think about, and in the following propagate, social contracts, or the one or other particular form/idea of a social contract of this or that nature.

detail.abstract: The best accident is the one that never happened. The best health care and best long-term care is the one that is not needed, because prevention prevented it. In social policy today, preventative approaches and goals are rare, and if mostly resort to lip service and lofty ideas, without concrete (actual) measures and consequences, without professional top priority given, without systemic applications, and without systematic, comprehensive and constant implementation. Prevention is feasible and the future of social policy depends on preventative social policy to take the lead, i.e. not to replace curative social policy, but to build the first track of social policy, besides curative social policy. Most modern mass diseases, as we know (should know) today, are preventable the very most part for the very most people (at least strongly delayable and reduceable). We have all sorts of workable (financeable, operable, and politically fully realistic) options to successfully, comprehensively, fully effectively and efficiently, and most important in a fully humane and decent manner, conduct preventative social policy. The political will will be there, once if the social policy awareness, practice and goals have been established and disseminated, accepted and wholeheartedly and continuously applied. Up to 90 percent (and more) of a great deal of modern mass diseases, the silent pandemics, are preventable if people start prevent them early in their lives and comprehensively, accumulating good healthy foods, drinks, exercise, happiness, sleep, social support, and buy preventing (avoiding) negative unhealthy foods and sugary/alcoholic drinks (including tobacco consumption), sedentary lifestyles, overweight, unhappiness, loneliness, social/cultural/economic/financial exclusion, etc. Hence, preventative health policy must become the mainstay of preventative social policy.

title: Thematic Meta Analysis in Social Policy Science

detail.title: Thematic Meta Analysis in Social Policy Science
detail.abstract: Each scientific discipline has to build and develop further discipline-specific methodology; i.e. to focus on, use and develop unique sets of methods that are designed to, or simply happen to, bring about progress in knowledge creation and deepening, as well as critical evaluations thereof. Social policy science is dealing with all sorts of problems that are mostly shared by countries, societies, communities all over the world, with at times great differences, and sometimes not. Social policy is also home to multi-layered, Lasagna-style social problems or societal problems, and scientific problems (in general) as well. Wicked causalities, wicked interactions, wicked hidden truths and hidden pasts, hidden side effects, hidden follow-on effects, all contribute to the need to upgrade analytical methodology. The word 'meta', in meta analysis, comes from Greek language and stands mostly for 'beyond,' i.e. beyond the usual, beyond the normal. Some studies are conceptualized at greater level-some abstract level, some global level, some grand-ourstorical(grand-historical) level, some try to tackle multilayered/multicyclical causalities, some are just so wide that they cover many more topics and themes in themselves, by themselves. These are all meta studies, using the method of (non-statistical) meta analysis, which here is understood as a social-policyscience-specific method (Aspalter, 2021). This has nothing to do with marketing, psychology, or medical science, etc., where different kinds of statistical meta analyses are applied, focusing on merging data and findings of other (a great, greater number of) studies. To be sure in social policy science, non-statistical meta analyses are very common, and super influential in bringing about progress, exploration, understanding and solutions (Aspalter, 2021). Grand themes, i.e. meta thematic analyses, are actually the main or most frequent choice of a great deal of social policy scientists.

title: Evolutionary Social Policy Theory: Its 8 Axioms, 6 Theorems

detail.title: Evolutionary Social Policy Theory: Its 8 Axioms, 6 Theorems
detail.abstract: For social policy science, we do not have such a marked tradition, as well as deep-and far-reaching theory. Yet, free after Thorstein Veblen (1898), we can throw up the following thought into the air: why is social policy science not an evolutionary science? For one, the recipients of social policy actions, protection, money and institutions, are recipients and not the prime actors per se. Social policy is the action of governments, who may or may not act upon the actions of people (protests, voting behaviors, survey, changing needs and demands, etc.). Thus, things are more complicated, but yet doable, when pointing the spotlight onto the politicians, administrators and experts themselves (see below). Historical analyses and historical case studies are always to greater or smaller degree evolutionary, upholding per definition (of what history does) a dynamic point of view, where time and history matters.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 247

detail.abstract: The surge of executive power unleashed by the Supreme Court has reached the Federal Reserve, provoking a crisis that the justices seem suddenly anxious to avoid. But the drama is long overdue. The central bank has a constitutional stature that poses a direct challenge to unitary executive theory, the principle animating the Court's recent case law. Congress established the Federal Reserve System to carry out a critical legislative prerogative-making the sovereign money supply. Congress used an institutional form-national banking-innovated precisely to secure sovereign money-making from executive (originally monarchical) interference. Congress in turn assigned a vital responsibility-the capacity to make money out of debt in the people's name-to the Fed. The constitutional conclusion follows: Congress's prerogative over money-making clearly secures the Fed's independence from presidential interference. That conclusion is lost in current scholarship that treats the Fed as fundamentally like other independent agencies. The Court has assumed, similarly, that the unitary executive presides over a relatively homogeneous regulatory field.  The case of the Fed exposes the separation of powers as a more complicated project.  Legislatures built democratic sovereignty by struggling for prerogatives that, like money-making, protected their lawmaking authority.  The prerogatives claimed by Congress inform the work of each agency and official, including within the executive branch.  The Court dismantles democratic sovereignty when it denies the reach of those prerogatives.

Digital programs and platforms, and of course increasingly important also AI (artificial intelligence) applications, machines and robots, are also quickly becoming mainstay operators of service delivery systems, including diagnosis, advice and health education. Pharmaceutical products, technical medical instruments; online applications; oneon-one communications; database creation and usage (harvesting and mining operations); knowledge creation, spread and applications; behavior analysis and guidance (through knowledge sharing in a humane, caring, careful, fully respectful manner), and of course health care personnel training and development are all part of the main imperatives of any health care systems.

detail.abstract: Federal diversity jurisdiction (jurisdiction over cases involving citizens of different U.S. states) is primarily justified by concern that state courts might be biased against out-of-state litigants. For at least one hundred years, however, this justification has been questioned by distinguished judges and academics, who have doubted whether such a bias exists or ever existed. This Article contains experimental evidence suggesting the existence of some bias against out-of-state defendants. The experimental evidence is bolstered by survey evidence showing that people admit that they prefer people from their own state and think out-of-state corporations are less concerned about safety. A survey of federal and state judges also shows that federal judges are more likely to police lawyer arguments that appeal to bias against out-of-state parties, which may help explain how federal diversity jurisdiction protects out-of-state litigants. Nevertheless, the evidence of bias and of differences between federal and state judges is not large or entirely consistent, suggesting that the bias rationale for federal jurisdiction is not strong.

title: What is the "Right" Geographic Market Definition?
affiliations: University of Cambridge, Cambridge Judge Business School and German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin)

detail.title: What is the "Right" Geographic Market Definition?
detail.abstract: This paper examines the "right" geographic definition of relevant markets by analyzing how excise tax pass-through varies with local competition in the retail gasoline market of a large metropolitan city. Using a natural experiment from three unanticipated and exogenous fuel tax hikes and detailed station-level price data, we show that average pass-through is invariant to the number of nearby competitors across various geographic definitions. This contrasts with theoretical predictions and prior island-based evidence, suggesting that the entire metropolitan area functions as a single market. Our findings challenge standard isodistance-or isochronebased market delineations used in academic research and competition policy.

title: Tariffs, Dollar Recycling, and U.S. Asset Valuations
affiliations: Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University

detail.title: Tariffs, Dollar Recycling, and U.S. Asset Valuations
detail.abstract: The United States runs persistent trade deficits that export dollars to the rest of the world. Foreign exporters and central banks reinvest these dollars in U.S. financial assets-a process we call dollar recycling. We argue that this recycling channel creates a structural demand premium for U.S. equities, contributing to the "exorbitant privilege" in asset valuations observed since the 1990s. Using an infinite-horizon two-country model with cash-in-advance constraints, we show that the trade-deficit-induced dollar overhang elevates U.S. price-dividend ratios above their frictionless benchmark in closed form: the equilibrium equity price equals the standard Gordon Growth benchmark divided by one minus the product of the recycling pass-through and the deficit-to-dividend ratio. Tariffs reduce bilateral deficits and compress this premium. We test the mechanism using event studies around eighteen major U.S. trade-policy announcements from 2018 to 2025. Countries with larger bilateral surpluses against the United States experience significantly more negative abnormal returns when tariff escalations are announced. A robustness analysis confirms that domestic investor rebalancing moderates-but does not eliminate-the valuation compression. Our model and evidence jointly indicate that tariff policy carries a financial-stability dimension that standard welfare analyses ignore.

detail.abstract: This paper studies debt-target reforms in a small open overlapping-generations economy with endogenous external spreads and productive public capital. We extend a tractable two-period benchmark to a finite horizon life cycle model with public debt and exact cohort welfare accounting. Lower debt targets can raise long-run growth while still imposing sizable welfare losses on cohorts alive at the reform date, and these effects operate mainly through human wealth and the consumption-scaling factor rather than financial revaluation. The open-economy margin is quantitatively important because reforms change the equilibrium path of net foreign liabilities and hence spreads and domestic interest rates, which materially shape both transition dynamics and cohort welfare.

When some households adjust only after threshold crossings, aggregate risk loads discontinuously onto frictionless households even though endowment evolves smoothly. The model implies skewness reversals at valuation extremes, asymmetric risk cycles, and state-dependent curvature at the short end of the yield curve. Closed-form asset prices obtain despite heterogeneous agents and inaction. U.S. equity data provide preliminary support for the skewness prediction, and Treasury evidence is consistent with, but more suggestive about, the model's front-end term-structure implication.

detail.abstract: This paper examines Nigeria's natural gas transportation infrastructure through the lens of the energy trilemma of energy security, energy equity, and environmental sustainability. Using a mixed-methods design, the study draws on two stakeholder surveys, literature review, and institutional analysis to assess how infrastructure development, governance, and management shape access to affordable natural gas and broader economic performance. The findings indicate that improved natural gas availability is associated with employment growth, stronger tax revenue, higher labour income, and a measurable contribution to GDP growth. At the same time, the sector is constrained by outdated pipelines, underinvestment, insecurity, policy inconsistency, and environmental risk. The study concludes that Nigeria requires stronger governance, greater regulatory clarity, continued infrastructure investment, and improved monitoring technologies if natural gas is to contribute meaningfully to inclusive and sustainable development.

title: The Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax and Financial Reporting Incentives
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford Graduate School of Business and Stanford University Graduate School of Business

detail.title: The Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax and Financial Reporting Incentives
detail.abstract: We develop a model to study how the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax (CAMT) affects firms' financial reporting behavior and their resulting tax burdens. We show that managers gradually reduce accrual-based earnings management as their book income exceeds the level that triggers the CAMT, which increases stock-price sensitivity to reported earnings. The CAMT's impact on reporting quality varies with managerial incentives: it improves this quality when managers prioritize stock prices, but reduces it when they focus on cash flows. However, it does not affect the informativeness of earnings. More profitable firms tend to pay a lower percentage of their income in CAMT, whereas firms with higher reporting precision and price-focused managers face a higher tax burden. We further study real earnings management, finding that it increases, rather than decreases, when the CAMT is triggered.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Sequential Testing with Heterogeneous LLMs
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, , Queen's University - Smith School of Business, , ,  and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Asymptotically Optimal Sequential Testing with Heterogeneous LLMs
detail.abstract: We study a Bayesian binary sequential hypothesis testing problem with multiple large language models (LLMs). Each LLM j has per-query cost c_j > 0, random waiting time with mean µ_j > 0 and sub-Gaussian tails, and asymmetric accuracies: the probability of returning the correct label depends on the true hypothesis θ ∈ {A, B} and needs not be the same under A and B. This asymmetry induces two distinct information rates (I_{j,A}, I_{j,B}) per LLM, one under each hypothesis. The decision-maker chooses LLMs sequentially, observes their noisy binary answers, and stops when the posterior probability of one hypothesis exceeds 1-α. The objective is to minimize the sum of expected query cost and expected waiting cost, E[C_π] + E[g(W_π)], where C_π is the total query cost, W_π is the total waiting time and g is a polynomial function (e.g., g(x) = x^ρ with ρ ≥ 1). We prove that as the error tolerance α → 0, the optimal policy is asymptotically equivalent to one that uses at most two LLMs. In this case, a single-LLM policy is not generically optimal: optimality now requires exploiting a two-dimensional tradeoff between information under A and information under B. Any admissible policy induces an expected information-allocation vector in R^2_+ , and we show that the optimal allocation lies at an extreme point of the associated convex set when α is relatively small, and hence uses at most two LLMs. We construct belief-dependent policies that first mix between two LLMs when the posterior is ambiguous, and then switch to a single "specialist" LLM when the posterior is sufficiently close to one of the hypotheses. These policies match the universal lower bound up to a (1 + o(1)) factor as α → 0.

title: A Polder Growth Model: Capital Wedges, Ecological Valuation Gaps and Social Leakages
affiliations: New College of Florida and University of Guyana

detail.title: A Polder Growth Model: Capital Wedges, Ecological Valuation Gaps and Social Leakages
detail.abstract: This paper presents the Polder Growth Model (PGM) to analyze the economic dynamics of societies situated in fragile coastal environments. The PGM includes a tripartite capital system – produced, human, and natural – where the latter represents both the physical integrity of the polder and the health of the coastal ecology. The model incorporates three distinct frictions: a capital (or infrastructure) wedge representing geographically imposed extra costs, a social leakage parameter capturing free-riding and institutional decay, and an ecological valuation gap reflecting the undervaluation of ecological services. We derive a steady-state per capita income characterized by a multiplier of fragility, demonstrating that environmental and social shocks are magnified in developed polder systems (levee paradox). Furthermore, we analyze the impact of exogenous resource rents (e.g., oil production), warning of a hollow production possibilities frontier where resource rents may hide the polder’s physical decline. We derive strong and weak sustainability rules, where the latter guides withdrawals from a Sovereign Wealth Fund (SWF) without mandatory minimum expenses to stay above water. The strong rule, our Polder Hartwick Rule, stipulates that resource rents must first surmount the necessary maintenance costs and depletion of ecological services (polder tax) before contributing to the next generation.

title: The Local Employment Effects of Pollution Abatement Infrastructure Investments

detail.title: The Local Employment Effects of Pollution Abatement Infrastructure Investments
detail.abstract: Large-scale environmental regulations and infrastructure mandates are often criticized as costly, yet evidence on their potential to generate local economic co-benefits is scarce. This paper estimates the local labor-market effects of the Clean Water Act (CWA) Construction Grants Program using a county-level staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting variation in the timing of first grant-assisted construction starts. Initiating construction raises construction employment by approximately twenty jobs per county-year over the first two post-treatment years, with accompanying increases in establishments and wages. Effects are disproportionately concentrated in smaller counties, indicating that the local impact of federal infrastructure spending depends on the size of the receiving economy. I also find significant responses in total employment and per-capita personal income, consistent with spillovers beyond the construction sector. Overall, the results show that environmental infrastructure investment can also generate short-run local economic gains.

title: Price depreciation and quality uncertainty for used battery electric vehicles

detail.title: Price depreciation and quality uncertainty for used battery electric vehicles
detail.abstract: We examine the formation of prices in the secondary market for Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs), where the ambiguity of battery health creates a valuation problem. Using a data set of 15,340 cars listed for sale in May 2024, we find that subsidized BEVs depreciate at a higher rate relative to gasoline cars. Our analysis of tax rate harmonization between fuel types indicates that consumer behavior is predominantly influenced by cost analysis rather than sustainability concerns. Our investigation of recalls shows that high-risk defects penalize a BEV significantly more than comparable gasoline cars.

detail.title: New Energy Demonstration Cities and the Mitigation of Energy Poverty in China
detail.abstract: China’s New Energy Demonstration Cities (NEDCs) sought to develop affordable, clean energy. This study therefore examines the NEDCs’ effectiveness in mitigating energy poverty (EP). We focus on electricity consumption, economic development, and renewable uptake – three components of International Energy Agency’s (IEA) measure of EP. Using panel data from 281 Chinese cities (2011-2021) and propensity score matching with difference-in-differences, the analysis found no statistically or economically significant overall effect of NEDCs on reducing EP. This is also consistent across the three IEA sub-components. The findings suggest this ineffectiveness may stem from weak enforcement, low public participation, and inequalities in income and education.

title: Accounting for Secure Software Development: Status, Trends and Business Focus: A Scoping Study
affiliations: Ton Duc Thang University

detail.title: Accounting for Secure Software Development: Status, Trends and Business Focus: A Scoping Study
detail.abstract: Secure software development is vital from both the developer and business perspectives. Although researchers have conducted studies examining specific aspects, no study has examined the overall status of, trends in and business focus regarding secure software development-a gap this study aims to fill. This study searched digital databases and identified 138 abstracts and 95 full articles. It conducted a scoping study and utilised NVivo software to generate themes, first from abstracts and then from source documents. It then analysed the top 25 themes to identify the current status of and trends in secure software development. The study then investigated the status of and trends in the business focus using the keyword 'business' alone. Results show a preponderance of themes that matched across the abstract and document analyses, with the most commonly discussed themes activities or processes related to secure software development. Although not present in the abstracts, source document analysis identified cybersecurity as one of the top 25 themes. There was minimal discussion on business focus, although it showed an upward trend over the project period. Journal articles and conference papers shared similar themes of significance; the book chapter themes differed, with cybersecurity the most frequently discussed theme.

title: The CEO Health Premium: Obesity Signals and Asset Pricing
affiliations: Shenzhen University WeBank Institute of Fintech and Shenzhen University - Shenzhen Audencia Business School

detail.title: The CEO Health Premium: Obesity Signals and Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: This paper documents that the physical appearance of CEOs, specifically excess body weight, is priced in the capital market. In the absence of explicit health disclosures, market participants interpret obesity as a proxy for latent health risks and potential managerial disrupts, thereby demanding a compensation premium. Our analysis reveals that (1) IPOs of firms with obese CEOs have lower first-day performance, (2) these firms achieve a lower valuation, (3) the stocks of these firms have lower liquidity and (4) they provide higher stock returns thereafter. A quasi-natural experiment based on the invention of anti-obesity medications provides supporting causal evidence.

title: When Climate Shapes Migration at Both Origin and Destination: Evidence from Tunisia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne and World Bank

detail.title: When Climate Shapes Migration at Both Origin and Destination: Evidence from Tunisia
detail.abstract: This paper examines internal and international migration as coping strategies to climate shocks in Tunisia, with a focus on agricultural channel. Using SPEI-based climate measures and the exhaustive 2014 Tunisian Population Census, we estimate pseudo-gravity models of internal migration incorporating push and pull factors, and a push-factor model of international emigration at the district level. We show that only accounting for origin-side effects would understate the overall impact of climate on migration by around 8\%. Over 2010–2014, climatic conditions are estimated to have induced roughly 3,000-6,000 additional internal migrants, and approximately 5,000-6,000 additional international emigrants, primarily along the France and Libya corridors. Migration responses are strongest in rural and high-cropland areas and among seasonal and agricultural workers, underscoring the role of agriculture in transmitting climate shocks into migration. Family ties outside the origin further facilitate climate migration by lowering migration costs. We also find evidence supporting the vulnerability hypothesis for internal migration, while international emigration increases under moderate drought but declines under severe drought, consistent with the resource-constraint hypothesis.

title: The Impact of Trade Wars on Firms in Third Countries
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The Impact of Trade Wars on Firms in Third Countries
detail.abstract: Bilateral trade shocks affect firms in third countries by simultaneously redirecting demand and reallocating competition across markets, creating winners and losers. We propose a general equilibrium trade model with heterogeneous firms to decompose firm-level export responses as a function of country-specific own-price and cross-price elasticities, and external economies of scale. Using the 2018–2019 US-China trade war as a source of exogenous variation and data on the universe of Italian firms, we show how bilateral trade shocks occurring elsewhere identify these primitives for third countries. On average, the US-China trade war created a 2.5% export gain, albeit with a standard deviation of 7.6% across firms. The largest gains accrued to more productive firms in sectors with stronger economies of scale, improving allocative efficiency.

title: The Information Used in Investment Decisions: Evidence from a Global Survey of Investment Professionals
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Accounting Group, The Ohio State University and University of Georgia - C. Herman and Mary Virginia Terry College of Business

detail.title: The Information Used in Investment Decisions: Evidence from a Global Survey of Investment Professionals
detail.abstract: We survey 793 investment professionals from around the globe to provide novel evidence on (1) the sources and types of information they use when making investment decisions, (2) the types of performance measures they use, and (3) their concerns about performance measures. Our evidence reveals the continued primacy of companies' financial reporting as an information source for investors. However, we also find that the majority of measures that investors use are not audited GAAP measures but instead alternative performance measures (APMs), such as non-GAAP financial measures (e.g., adjusted earnings), financial KPIs (e.g., same store sales), and operating KPIs (e.g., number of subscribers). Investors' primary concern about these APMs is their comparability, which is understudied in academic research. Our evidence has implications for the resources spent in different areas of scholarly inquiry, for instructional time in the classroom, and for standard setting and regulation of companies' financial reporting.

title: AI Infrastructure and Regional Electricity Demand:Evidence from U.S. Interconnection Queues

detail.title: AI Infrastructure and Regional Electricity Demand:Evidence from U.S. Interconnection Queues

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no conflicts of interest to declare
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Data sources used are publicly available: EIA Form 930, LBNL Queued Up (2024), NOAA NCEI, and BEA Regional Accounts.

detail.abstract:
Between 2019 and 2025, electricity demand in ERCOT, the Texas grid, grew by roughly
27 percent. In PJM and MISO, the two largest electricity markets in the country, demand
was essentially flat. This divergence coincides with the largest surge in data center
investment in American history and with ERCOT interconnection queue filings that
reached 97 gigawatts in 2024 alone. This paper asks how much of that divergence data
center investment can explain, and whether the existing investment pipeline is large
enough to stress the grid in ways that current planning models are not built to anticipate. I
combine hourly electricity demand data from the EIA with interconnection queue data
compiled by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the University of Maryland to
build a four-layer identification strategy: panel regression, synthetic control, difference-in-
differences with low-exposure controls, and narrative validation against known data
center energization dates. The main empirical result is a 34.8 index-point divergence in
ERCOT minimum hourly demand above a synthetic counterfactual built from balancing
authorities with low data center exposure; the baseload floor signature of infrastructure
that maintains high minimum power draw regardless of weather or time of day. A three model
forecasting pipeline (ARIMA, Prophet, XGBoost) estimated on ERCOT zone-level
data produces scenario projections through 2027 and quantifies the informational
value of the generation-side queue proxy. Clean causal identification is not currently
possible. The project-level large load queue data that would make it possible does not
exist as a public record in any major U.S. electricity market. I document this absence as a
policy finding and argue it represents a significant gap in public oversight of the grid.

title: Policy credibility and speculation in the EU ETS
affiliations: , University of Bologna and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Policy credibility and speculation in the EU ETS
detail.abstract: Speculation and policy credibility are increasingly debated as drivers of EU ETS price dynamics, yet they are typically analysed separately. This is problematic because credibility and speculation interact through firms’ banking and compliance decisions: doubts about future policy weaken banking and depress prices, while speculative trading can amplify price movements and feed back into perceived credibility by shaping abatement incentives and realised emissions. We develop a dynamic behavioural model in which credibility evolves endogenously with ETS performance. Compliance firms choose abatement and bank more when credibility is higher,while heterogeneous financial traders take positions in permit futures using fundamentalist and trend-following expectations, alongside noise trading. We show that a policy-anchored equilibrium is locally stable when credibility-sensitive banking provides a strong anchor, but self-fulfilling speculative equilibria emerge when trend-following dominates. Calibrated simulations for 2023–2050 indicate that fundamentals-anchored trading can reinforce credibility, support higher prices and abatement, and reduce cumulative emissions, while a reform to the Market Stability Reserve scaling thresholds with the declining cap improves late-transition control over the net-zero date.

title: Re-Globalization via Capital account Liberalization: Argentina's Capital Controls and Sovereign Debt re-Negotiations under Macri
affiliations: Boston University, Metropolitan College (MET) and Bridgewater State University

detail.title: Re-Globalization via Capital account Liberalization: Argentina's Capital Controls and Sovereign Debt re-Negotiations under Macri
detail.abstract: Globalization as a discourse has the power to shape economic policy and its underlying logics. By conceptualizing re-globalization as a discursive mechanism, the paper contributes to the extant literature of financialization and globalization. Thus, theoretically the paper contributes to the financialization literature by integrating discursive factors into the analysis of structural policy change. The empirical case study examines Argentine President Mauricio Macri's economic policy plan to re-globalize and how it was framed by the Argentine financial press. It examines the discourses deployed by the financial press towards generating legitimacy and consent. The case provides an empirical evaluation of how these deregulation strategies resulted in policy changes leading to inflationary pressures, capital flight, and currency depreciation pass-through early in his administration. It serves as a test case to explain how discourses can aPect policy outcomes. The analysis further demonstrates how capital controls and the lifting thereof-can either buPer or accelerate the ePects of globalized finance.

title: Poisoned Fruits: The Legacy of Arsenic Pesticides in the Early Twentieth-Century United States

detail.title: Poisoned Fruits: The Legacy of Arsenic Pesticides in the Early Twentieth-Century United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: This paper provides the first systematic evidence on the health consequences of arsenic-based pesticides, the dominant insecticides in U.S. agriculture until 1945. I digitize county rural vital statistics and link them to historical pesticide use in apple orchards. I find that exposed areas experienced an increase in rural infant mortality. Linking Army enlistment records to census manuscripts, I show that exposed cohorts were shorter on average. Distinguishing trees by farm and production status, I show the effects are driven by pesticide use rather than orchard presence. Groundwater data reveal lasting contamination, underscoring the environmental legacy of the early chemical revolution.

title: What Matters More for Emerging Markets Investors: Economic Growth or EPS Growth?
affiliations: , Research Affiliates, Rayliant Global Advisors, University of Florida - Department of Finance, Insurance and Real Estate and Independent

detail.title: What Matters More for Emerging Markets Investors: Economic Growth or EPS Growth?
detail.abstract: Investors often allocate to emerging markets equities with the expectation that higher rates of gross domestic product (GDP) growth typical of developing economies will translate to better stock market returns. Adherents to this conventional wisdom have historically been disappointed, as numerous studies of emerging and developed markets have shown GDP growth to be unreliable in predicting country-level stock returns. Using data from 15 emerging and 21 developed equity markets over samples ranging from 32 to 120 years, we confirm the failure of GDP growth as a cross-sectional predictor. What truly matters to investors is not an overall increase in economic output but rather the growth in listed companies’ earnings per share (EPS) and dividends per share (DPS), which ultimately flows to shareholders. We confirm that, unlike changes in GDP, growth in EPS and DPS exhibit a strong positive correlation with country-level equity returns, offering emerging markets investors a more effective tool for thinking about allocation decisions. Surprisingly, we also find that most emerging economies, despite their high GDP growth rate, have low EPS and DPS growth rates, suggesting that listed companies are not representative of the underlying economy.

title: Retained Surgical Instrument Following Cesarean Section: A Case of Diagnostic Delay, Marital Strain, and Medical Negligence

detail.title: Retained Surgical Instrument Following Cesarean Section: A Case of Diagnostic Delay, Marital Strain, and Medical Negligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Retained surgical items following caesarean section represent preventable 'Never Events' with significant clinical and legal ramifications. This case involved a twelve-month diagnostic delay compounded by fraudulent concealment of radiological records, resulting in profound psychosocial sequelae including marital dissolution. We analysed the diagnostic delay, legal liability frameworks, and systemic failures, with particular emphasis on the Statutory Duty of Candour and secondary victim claims. Using doctrinal legal methodology, we examined the Bolam/Bolitho tests for negligence, the 'but-for' and material contribution tests for causation, and the Alcock criteria for secondary victim claims under English law. Our analysis establishes a threefold breach of duty: the initial retained surgical instrument constitutes res ipsa loquitur negligence; the twelve-month diagnostic delay fails the Bolitho test of logical defensibility; and fraudulent concealment engages Section 32 of the Limitation Act 1980. The marital dissolution satisfies criteria for recognised psychiatric injury and loss of amenity under the Judicial College Guidelines. This case demonstrates that retained surgical item litigation must extend beyond compensatory damages to address systemic governance failures. Implementation of blockchain-verified radiological audit trails and RFID-tagged surgical instruments will prevent similar occurrences and ensure the Statutory Duty of Candour operates as a technologically-enforced mandate.

This paper examines a serious medical error where a surgical needle was accidentally left inside a woman's uterus after an emergency caesarean section. What made this case worse was that when the patient complained of ongoing pain, her doctor deliberately gave her another person's medical scan to hide the mistake. This delayed proper diagnosis for a full year, causing prolonged physical suffering and eventually leading to the breakdown of her marriage. We analyse the legal responsibilities of doctors and hospitals in such cases, and argue that modern technology--such as tamper-proof medical records and surgical instruments with tracking chips--could prevent similar incidents. The case highlights why doctors must be honest with patients when errors occur, rather than trying to cover them up.

detail.title: Beyond Nudges: AI Agents, Antitrust, and Complexity Economics

publicationDetails.detailsText: Amsterdam Law & Technology Institute Working Paper Series, 2026

detail.abstract: Behavioral economics is the intuitive framework for analyzing AI agents and chatbot-induced challenges in antitrust. It is the insufficient one. The analytical puzzle AI agents pose for antitrust has three dimensions: how recommendations shape consumer beliefs about products and markets; how AI agent architectures interact with and reshape the preferences that guide consumer choice; and how recommendation-driven markets alter market dynamics in ways that may or may not produce competitive harm. BE sees primarily the first. Complexity economics sees all three.

title: Is Mandatory Climate Risk Disclosure Relevant to Investors? Evidence for Stock returns in the UK
affiliations: WHU - Otto Beisheim School of Management and WHU Otto Beisheim Graduate School of Management

detail.title: Is Mandatory Climate Risk Disclosure Relevant to Investors? Evidence for Stock returns in the UK
detail.abstract: We assess whether the introduction of mandatory climate-related financial disclosure rules in the UK has influenced the risk premium of companies. The shift to mandatory disclosure rules is relevant as previous research has considered voluntary disclosure to be insufficient. Using the large language model climateBERT to measure transition or physical climate risk reporting, we find that the new regulation has significantly increased the level of disclosure on both risk types. This finding also holds for companies previously supporting voluntary disclosure based on the TCFD framework. However, our results show that the increase in reporting due to the regulation had no significant impact on stock returns. Changes in reporting were only related to stock returns in the period before the mandatory disclosure regulation was announced.

title: How Pedestrians React to Imminent Vehicle Threats: A Virtual Reality Study in Safety-Critical Scenarios
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tsinghua University - State Key Laboratory of Automotive Safety and Energy and Tsinghua University - State Key Laboratory of Automotive Safety and Energy

detail.title: How Pedestrians React to Imminent Vehicle Threats: A Virtual Reality Study in Safety-Critical Scenarios
detail.abstract: As vulnerable road users, pedestrians sustain high collision risk in safety-critical traffic scenarios. When faced with approaching vehicles, pedestrians need to balance their road crossing desire with the demands for safety, resulting in either normal walking or avoidance behaviors. Such uncertain behavior affects the occurrence of collisions. Therefore, it is important to understand pedestrian natural behaviors so that highly automated vehicles (HAVs) can better develop safe interaction or effective protective strategies. To study these behaviors under controlled conditions, we designed an immersive virtual reality (VR) experiment where participants encountered traffic scenarios with different spatiotemporal pressures. The experiment has revealed three distinct behavior modes under increasing spatiotemporal pressures: a no-risk mode driven solely by the desire of crossing road, a game mode balancing safety and crossing desire, and a life-saving mode prioritizing collision avoidance. Based on these behavior modes, we proposed a regression model to predict pedestrian decisions. The model achieved average precision of 0.87 and 0.82 for predicting whether and how pedestrian avoid. Finally, real pedestrian-vehicle conflict data are used to validate the effectiveness of the experimental results. This investigation clarifies pedestrians’ behavior modes in various urgent scenarios and presents a decision model based on pedestrians’ behavior modes, detailing their interaction logic with hazardous vehicles in traffic scenarios. We expect that the observed behavior modes can help develop safety algorithms of HAVs to make safe interactions with pedestrians on roads.

detail.title: How Economic Policy Uncertainty Spreads across Borders: The case of Latin America

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2549
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Latin America’s growth has been hindered by institutional instability and volatile economic policies, often driven by political cycles. These shifts generate uncertainty that deters investment and disrupts productivity. We analyze this phenomenon using Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) indices, assessing their impact on domestic macroeconomic variables via regional spillovers - spurred by regional proximity - and also considering the global transmission of EPU shocks to key trade and financial partners. To do so, we assemble a comprehensive and comparable database of EPU indices for the region: first, we construct new indices for Bolivia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Uruguay and Venezuela, and second, we update the ones available in other papers for Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru using a comparable methodology. Our results show that: (i) regional EPU shocks reduce regional GDP growth, deter capital inflows and spark exchange rate instability; (ii) Brazil and Mexico are key sources of uncertainty spillovers within the region; and (iii) EPU shocks in Latin America affect financial and real variables in major partner economies, with Spain being particularly exposed.

detail.abstract: We study the evolution of intergenerational educational mobility and related distributional statistics in Spain. Over recent decades, mobility has risen by one-third, coinciding with pronounced declines in inequality and assortative mating among the same cohorts. To explore these patterns, we examine regional correlates of mobility, using split-sample techniques. A key finding from both national and regional analyses is the close association between mobility and assortative mating: spousal sorting accounts for nearly half of the regional variation in intergenerational correlations and also appears to be a key mediator of the negative relationship between inequality and mobility documented in recent studies.
