detail.abstract: Urban healthcare accessibility remains a critical challenge in rapidly developing cities, where disparities in socioeconomic status often correlate with inequitable access to medical facilities. This study addresses the Uncapacitated Facility Location Problem for healthcare infrastructure planning in Delhi, India, using real-world road network data and multi-objective optimization techniques. A computational framework was developed that integrates OpenStreetMap road network data with simulated socioeconomic constraints to model healthcare accessibility under realistic traffic conditions. Two optimization approaches were implemented and compared: a greedy heuristic algorithm comparing efficiency-only versus equity-weighted objectives, and the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) for simultaneous multi-objective optimization. The NSGA-II approach generated a Pareto front of 100 optimal solutions, revealing a fundamental trade-off between minimizing average travel time (efficiency) and minimizing the Gini coefficient of travel times (equity). Results demonstrate that equity-weighted optimization shifts facility placement toward peripheral, lower-socioeconomic areas, reducing average travel time for underserved populations by up to 15% compared to efficiency-only solutions. The best compromise solution achieved an average travel time of 437.1 seconds with a Gini coefficient of 0.246, effectively balancing both objectives. This framework provides policymakers with quantitative tools for evidence-based healthcare infrastructure planning that explicitly incorporates social equity considerations.

title: Mandatory Pay Disclosures in Job Postings
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE), Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE),  and

detail.title: Mandatory Pay Disclosures in Job Postings
detail.abstract: We investigate the economic consequences of mandating salary range disclosures in job postings in Colorado, Washington, and California. We find a sizable increase in salary range disclosure, although 25 percent of job postings appear to omit pay information post-mandate. However, this non-disclosure does not appear to be strategically motivated, nor does the width of disclosed salary ranges vary with firms' incentives to provide uninformative ranges. In line with the informative nature of mandated pay disclosures, we find evidence of increased pay levels in general, and a reduction in gender pay gaps in particular, especially when pay transparency increases are more pronounced. Contrary to voiced concerns, we find no increase in biased pay perceptions. Finally, we document negative market reactions to the announcement of these mandates and an increase in firm-level expenses, suggesting that the mandates impose net costs onto regulated firms. Our findings offer nuanced insights into the multifaceted impacts of pay transparency laws, highlighting both their societal benefits and financial consequences for firms.

detail.abstract: This working paper examines the influence of artificial intelligence classification on valuation dynamics and capital allocation in global technology mergers and acquisitions between 2022 and 2025. Using a sample of publicly disclosed transactions, the study compares enterprise value multiples across AI-native firms, AI-enabled incumbents, and non-AI technology companies. The analysis incorporates descriptive statistics and regression modelling to evaluate the relative explanatory power of revenue growth, EBITDA margins, and AI classification on observed valuation outcomes. The findings suggest that while AI exposure is associated with valuation dispersion, growth quality and margin profile remain more statistically significant determinants of transaction pricing. The paper further examines structural deal trends, including earnout design, regulatory scrutiny, and integration risk in AI-driven acquisitions. Implications are discussed for private equity sponsors, corporate acquirers, and policy observers evaluating capital allocation decisions in 2026. This paper relies exclusively on publicly available transaction data and institutional research.

title: Automated Market Making with Continuity: Liquidity, Price Discovery, and Adverse Selection
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, University of Houston - Department of Finance and The University of Texas at San Antonio, Alvarez College of Business

detail.title: Automated Market Making with Continuity: Liquidity, Price Discovery, and Adverse Selection
detail.abstract: Constant-Product Automated Market Makers (CPAMMs) are an established mechanism for trading crypto-assets and may soon support trading of tokenized equities. We develop a minimal-structure model in which traders' strategies and valuations are continuous. Despite its simplicity, the model delivers a rich set of sharp predictions. CPAMM markets provide incentives for perfectly competitive liquidity provision. Equilibrium prices are invariant to liquidity supply. Traders' valuations can be recovered linearly from reserves and transaction prices, allowing variation in traders' motivations to be decomposed into information-driven and liquidity-driven trading components. A simple equilibrium relation links liquidity provision, price spreads, and price impact; and the model provides a closedform measure of expected adverse selection costs. We test these predictions using Uniswap V2 as the CPAMM market and Binance as the alternative market. Consistent with the theory, Uniswap reserves Granger-predict trading volume, estimated relationships among reserves, price spreads, and slippage have the predicted signs, and adverse selection costs are positively related to the variance of the permanent (information-driven) component of valuations.

title: Predicting Cost-Related Delays in Medical Care: A Temporally Validated, Fairness-Aware Machine Learning Analysis of CDC BRFSS Data (2016-2022)

detail.abstract: Cost-related delays in medical care represent a persistent and inequitably distributed barrier to health access in the United States. We present a reproducible machine learning pipeline trained on four cycles of the CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS; 2016-2019; N ≈ 2.1 million) and evaluated via strict temporal holdout on the 2022 survey (N = 443,523; survey-weighted prevalence = 11.1%). Three classifiers-logistic regression, random forest, and LightGBM-were trained with survey-weighted cross-validation and isotonic calibration. All models achieved test-set AUROC of 0.788-0.792 (bootstrap 95% CIs spanning ≤ 0.01), with ∆AUROC < 0.005 from cross-validation, confirming low temporal drift over 2016-2022. Decision curve analysis shows positive net benefit across a clinically relevant threshold range of 5-35%. Fairness analysis revealed systematic disparities: AUROC ranged from 0.719 to 0.804 across racial/ethnic subgroups and from 0.760 to 0.795 across income strata, with consistent gradients across all three model families. SHAP attribution identified age, income, insurance status, and-most notably-survey non-response on the mental health item as the dominant predictors, surfacing informative missingness as an underappreciated signal in population health surveys. These findings demonstrate that cost-related access barriers are predictable and temporally stable, but that a globally trained model distributes predictive accuracy inequitably across demographic subgroups.

title: The Fokker-Planck Calculus in Quantitative Finance
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: The Fokker-Planck Calculus in Quantitative Finance
detail.abstract: This paper develops a rigorous, unified framework for Fokker-Planck methods in quantitative finance, organized around four structurally distinct analytical regimes. First, in the reversible spectral regime, we establish that generator self-adjointness on L 2 (π θ) holds if and only if the diffusion satisfies a divergence-form reversibility condition, yielding a complete Schrödinger spectral theory with exponential convergence at the Poincaré rate. Second, for the CIR-Laguerre regime, we show that every one-dimensional diffusion is inherently reversible with respect to its speed measure, requiring no Doob h-transform; a simple rescaling reduces the CIR generator to the classical Laguerre operator with explicit spectral expansions. Third, in the affine-Fourier regime, we provide a corrected derivation of the Heston Riccati system, restoring the missing log-price drift term and placing the factor iw exclusively in the initial condition. Fourth, the signature-generator correspondence is established via Dynkin's formula and Ni's backward PDE hierarchy, clarifying that higher-level expected signatures cannot be obtained by naive semigroup factorization due to quadratic variation effects. Additional contributions include a four-term spectral Fisher information formula, the JKO variational structure with non-constant mobility, and a local convergence theorem for natural-gradient calibration. Several errors in recent literature are identified and corrected throughout.

detail.abstract: The U.S. credit-card economy is a platform-scale decision system. Still, it lacks a neutral decision operating system (Decision OS) at the two moments when value is created and allocated: checkout (which payment instrument is used, and which offer/reward is captured) and repayment (which balances are revolved, paid down, or refinanced, and when). In 2024 alone, consumer credit card purchase volume reached $3.6T and balances exceeded $1.2T, while consumers were assessed $160B in interest charges and paid $31.3B in fees (including $17B in late fees), reflecting record APRs and increasing minimum-payment behavior [1]. In parallel, merchants paid $187.20B in card-acceptance fees to accept $11.902T in card payments, underscoring that checkout is already supported by enormous, ongoing budgets [2]. This paper proposes LXMQ, a Decision OS that routes value across the consumer issuer merchant ecosystem via a unified financial hypergraph (consumer card merchant entities and events) and a six-algorithm architecture: (i) a unified data fabric and feature graph; (ii) an adaptive spend optimizer at checkout; (iii) a dynamic pay-down scheduler for multi-card repayment; (iv) a neural rewards amplifier for valuation-aware points redemption; (v) a predictive fee-alert guardian; and (vi) a real-time credit health predictor and simulator. LXMQ is positioned as an infrastructure-layer system that can be distributed directly to consumers or embedded via partner applications, aligning with emerging standardized data-access regimes [3].

title: The Nexus between the Deposit and Risk-Taking Channels of Monetary Policy
affiliations: Banco de España, Banco de España and Banco de España

detail.title: The Nexus between the Deposit and Risk-Taking Channels of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the deposit channel of monetary policy during the fastest and most intense tightening cycle of the Euro era. Using the universal Spanish credit register and regional variation in deposit market concentration, we show that limited pass-through of policy rates to deposit rates-driven by banks' regional market power-produces heterogeneous effects on bank credit supply and risk-taking. Following the tightening cycle, banks operating in more concentrated deposit markets reduced credit more sharply to riskier firms. For newly originated loans, this contraction was accompanied by higher interest rates and improved realized returns. We document a novel dimension of the deposit channel: it compels banks to actively optimize their risk-return trade-off. Our results show that preserving deposit franchise value leads banks to prioritize prudence, reversing the "search-for-yield" dynamic observed during the zero-lower-bound era.

title: Emotion in Euro Area Monetary Policy Communication and Bond Yields: The Draghi Era

detail.abstract: We combine modern methods from Speech Emotion Recognition and Natural Language Processing with high-frequency financial data to analyze how the vocal emotions and language of ECB President Mario Draghi affect the yields and yield spreads of major euro area economies. This novel approach to central bank communication reveals that vocal and verbal emotions significantly impact the yield curve, with effects varying in magnitude and direction. Our results reveal an important asymmetry in yield changes with positive signals raising German, French, and Spanish yields, while negative cues increase Italian yields. Our analysis of bond spreads and equity markets indicates that positive communication influences the risk-free yield component, whereas negative communication affects the risk premium. Additionally, our study contributes by constructing a synchronized dataset for voice and language analysis.

detail.abstract: Introduction: The adoption of International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) is increasingly central to public financial management (PFM) reform agendas across sub-Saharan Africa. Ghana, which has invested substantially in PFM infrastructure-including the Ghana Integrated Financial Management Information System (GIFMIS)-represents an important case for understanding the practitioner-level experience of IPSAS implementation. Despite growing policy momentum, empirical evidence on the perceptions, challenges, and implementation outcomes from the perspective of frontline public sector professionals remains limited. This study examines the awareness, perceived benefits, implementation challenges, and outlook of IPSAS adoption among public sector practitioners in Ghana. It further investigates whether perceptions vary across organisation types and experience levels. Methods: A structured online questionnaire was administered to 400 public sector practitioners across five organisation types in Ghana (central government ministries, audit institutions, local governments, regulatory bodies, and public corporations). Quantitative data were analysed using Python (v3.12) with the pandas, NumPy, scipy, seaborn, and matplotlib libraries. Descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, frequency distributions) one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), and Pearson correlation analysis were computed for all survey items. Results: Respondents demonstrated strong awareness of IPSAS (M = 4.24) and broadly endorsed the necessity of PFM reforms (M = 4.70). IPSAS was perceived as a key component of Ghana's reform agenda (M = 4.48). Over 72.5% of respondents reported either full or partial IPSAS implementation in their organisations. Perceived benefits were consistently high across comparability (M = 4.52), reliability (M = 4.28), and donor confidence (M = 4.32). Principal implementation challenges included capacity and training deficits (M = 4.00), system incompatibility (M = 3.56), and legal/regulatory misalignment (M = 3.51). Outlook was strongly positive, with respondents anticipating IPSAS's contribution to international bestpractice alignment (M = 4.50) and fiscal discipline (M = 4.36). ANOVA revealed no statistically significant differences in perceptions across organisation types (p > 0.10), suggesting broad consensus. Discussion: Ghanaian public sector practitioners hold strongly favourable views towards IPSAS adoption. The primary barriers are systemic and structural-particularly inadequate training, technological incompatibility, and regulatory gaps-rather than fundamental disagreements about the value of reform. These findings carry important implications for policymakers seeking to accelerate IPSAS full adoption in Ghana and comparable low-and middle-income country contexts.

title: Evaluation of the International Management of Mutual Funds
affiliations: and Universidad Europea de Madrid

detail.title: Evaluation of the International Management of Mutual Funds
detail.abstract: The collective investment industry has experienced significant growth in the last decade. Simultaneously, there has been a sharp increase in the internationalization of mutual fund portfolios. In this context, the objective of this study is to analyze, in 35 countries around the world, the relationship between the degree of internationalization of the portfolio and the level of fund efficiency. Different performance measures, or results evaluations, are applied to portfolio management. The results reveal significant differences in fund efficiency, with domestic funds achieving better results than international funds. However, when considering the effect of size, the results show a negative (positive) relationship between the degree of internationalization of the fund and its efficiency for lower (higher) levels of assets. Furthermore, in aggregate terms, no synchronization capacity of the funds is evident. However, it is found that the ability to synchronize with the international market is lower than that with the domestic market.

title: ML-Based ESG Score Prediction in Indian Banking Sector and Finance Sector (2015-2025)
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: ML-Based ESG Score Prediction in Indian Banking Sector and Finance Sector (2015-2025)
detail.abstract:
This research analyzes and develops machine learning models that will predict the ESG score for 48 of the largest banks and non-banking financial companies in India between 2015 and 2025 (528 firm-years). The models use various data types (such as financial metrics, governance, regulatory compliance and trends over time). The machine learning model used, XGBoost, produced significantly better results than traditional linear regression models when predicting the ESG score of the corresponding firms with an R² of 0.79, a RMSE of 4.7 and a MAE of 3.6 based on out-of-time test data (2023 through 2025).

SHAP analysis has identified that the primary drivers of ESG performance are board independence (21.8%), firm size (18.4%), regulatory trends (15.2%) and return on assets (12.7%) respectively. When comparing private sector banks to public sector banks, the private sector banks' ESG scores were better on average by 8 to 15 ESG points (68.4 vs 55.7). The ESG scores of the entire sector have increased 51% (47.2 to 71.5) over the period from 2015 to 2025, primarily due to the introduction of SEBI's BRSR framework (2021) and RBI's climate risk guidelines.

The results of this research allow for data-driven forecasts of ESG performance in emerging markets that are developing new disclosure requirements, and thus provide valuable information for investors, regulators and financial institutions. Limitations of this study include data sparsity prior to 2022, possible endogeneity between financial performance and ESG scores, and methodological differences across agencies.

title: The Spatial Incidence of Hyperscale Data Centers
affiliations: , , University of Calgary - Finance and Business School, National University of Singapore

detail.title: The Spatial Incidence of Hyperscale Data Centers
detail.abstract: We estimate the local incidence of U.S. data center openings using stacked difference-in-differences design and nationwide housing transaction data. We find that hyperscale data centers--those owned and operated by large cloud/AI firms--reduce nearby house prices by 6.8 percent, with effects highly localized and fading beyond 14 km. These effects increase with power capacity and attenuate with prior local exposure. By contrast, large non-hyperscale facilities show little evidence of capitalization, suggesting that burden intensity alone is not sufficient. Taken together, our results indicate that the local incidence of digital infrastructure depends on operating model and siting context, not scale alone. These findings have direct implications for the evaluation of data center subsidies and siting policy.

title: On Physician Overconfidence
affiliations: Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine,  and University of Cologne - Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences

detail.title: On Physician Overconfidence
detail.abstract: We study overconfidence and its consequences among 1,050 physicians in Ghana, representing about 10 percent of the country's physician workforce. Using a lab-in-the-field experiment with incentivized clinical vignettes and beliefs about relative performance, we find that 47 percent of physicians are overconfident. We observe that overconfidence is at least partly formed rationally, as tests fail to reject Bayesian updating while posterior beliefs are better calibrated than priors. We obtain evidence for motivated beliefs as a driver of overconfidence as physicians selectively seek feedback about their performance, especially when they expect to have performed well. This pattern is strongest among the overconfident and consistent with self-image concerns. Physicians also exhibit strong social image concerns, albeit these concerns are not limited to the overconfident. Overall, physician overconfidence appears closely tied to self-image motivesthe intrinsic desire to be a good doctor-and does not reduce performance. Important consequences of physician overconfidence for the use of clinical decision-support systems and team decision rules are also investigated.

title: Data Assets and Firm Value

detail.title: Data Assets and Firm Value

detail.abstract: We examine the equity market and real effects of mandatory data asset recognition using a regulatory shock in China. On August 21, 2023, China's Ministry of Finance issued the Data Resource Interim Provisions, requiring listed firms to recognize qualifying data resources as balance sheet assets — the first such mandate globally — effective January 1, 2024. Using this mandate as a quasi-natural experiment, we find that data-asset firms realize a 2.11 percent cumulative abnormal return over a four-day event window. The effect is stronger for financially constrained firms, firms with higher SG&A and R&D expenditures, state-owned enterprises, and firms with more advanced digital transformation, consistent with investors anticipating real economic benefits rather than mere accounting reclassification. Data-asset firms subsequently experience improved financing access, increased investment in R&D and organizational capital, and better operating performance. Financial statement data from 2024Q1 to 2025Q3 document rapid growth in data asset recognition, with limited balance sheet effects but meaningful impacts on operating expenses and earnings. Our findings inform ongoing global standard-setting debates on internally generated intangibles and suggest that the economic consequences of recognition depend critically on the surrounding institutional environment.

title: Racial Epithets And Title Vii Hostile Work Environment Claims: Case Commentary On Smith V. P.A.M. Transport (6TH CIR. 2025)
affiliations: University of New Mexico - School of Law and

detail.title: Racial Epithets And Title Vii Hostile Work Environment Claims: Case Commentary On Smith V. P.A.M. Transport (6TH CIR. 2025)
detail.abstract: In order to rule fairly in employment discrimination cases, courts cannot adhere to rigid categories of harassment. In Smith v. P.A.M. Transport, Inc., two plaintiffs sued their employer under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act after a supervisor of the same race as the employees referred to each of them by the term, “monkey ass.” The plaintiffs also claimed that their supervisors cursed, threatened, and shouted at them while treating white employees with respect. After the district court granted summary judgment in favor of the defendant, the Sixth Circuit reversed. The Sixth Circuit reasoned that “monkey ass” is a racial slur because of its history and usage, that employment discrimination plaintiffs do not need to prove the racial self-identification of workplace comparators, and that the race of the supervisor does not obviate the severity of the harassment without more evidence. In addition, we address the concurring opinion’s use of ChatGPT by exploring whether large language models can help courts determine the meanings of racially sensitive, composite phrases in the context of employment discrimination. Overall, the Sixth Circuit embraced an interpretation of Title VII that acknowledges the nuance and factual complexity of workplace interactions, thus allowing plaintiffs to articulate claims in language that is familiar to them.

title: Reserve Demand Estimation with Minimal Theory
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Reserve Demand Estimation with Minimal Theory

publicationDetails.detailsText: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Papers, volume 26, issue 07, 2026[10.21144/wp26-07]

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We propose a new reserve-demand estimation strategy—a middle ground between atheoretical reduced-form econometric approaches and fully structural quantitative-theoretic approaches. The strategy consists of an econometric specification that satisfies core restrictions implied by theory and controls for changes in administered-rate spreads that induce rotations and shifts in reserve demand. The resulting approach is as user-friendly as existing reduced-form econometric methods but improves upon them by incorporating a minimal set of theoretical restrictions that any reserve demand must satisfy. We apply this approach to U.S. data and obtain reserve-demand estimates that are broadly consistent with the structural estimates in Lagos and Navarro (2023).

title: Signaling Effects of Government Spending: The Financing Schemes Matter
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - School of Finance and Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - China Economics and Management Academy

detail.title: Signaling Effects of Government Spending: The Financing Schemes Matter
detail.abstract: Government spending may affect households not only through expected demand stimulus but also by revealing policymakers' private information about economic fundamentals. We study whether households interpret expansionary fiscal policy as such a signal of weaker future economic fundamentals (signaling effect), and whether the signaling effect depends on how the spending is financed. We first develop a stylized signal-extraction model in which the government chooses both the size of spending and the tax share of financing in response to its private information about underlying conditions. Guided by this model, we conduct a large-scale survey experiment that varies both the size and financing of fiscal expansions. Debt-financed spending leads households to revise expectations pessimistically, lowering expected GDP growth and raising perceived recession risk, while tax-financed spending generates substantially weaker responses. These effects are driven by policy surprises and are concentrated among respondents who believe the government possesses superior information. Consistent with a signaling mechanism, debt-financed expansions also increase perceived economic weakness and reduce willingness to purchase durable goods. A robustness wave using alternative fiscal vignettes confirms these patterns. Our findings provide direct evidence that fiscal policy influences expectations and behavior not only through direct stimulus effects but also through an informational channel shaped by financing choices.

title: Clientelism, Institutions and Sovereign Default
affiliations: SUNY Stony Brook - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Clientelism, Institutions and Sovereign Default

publicationDetails.detailsText: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Papers, volume 26, issue 06, 2026[10.21144/wp26-06]

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Emerging economies exhibit pro-cyclical fiscal policy, counter-cyclical sovereign spreads, and recurrent debt crises, whereas advanced economies sustain high debt with low spreads and lower volatility in outcomes. We document that these differences are systematically related to institutional strength, measured by horizontal accountability, and to the prevalence of clientelistic allocation of public resources in a panel of 51 countries (1994-2023). We develop a dynamic political-economy model of sovereign borrowing with long-term debt in which institutional constraints discipline clientelistic transfers and shape default incentives. Variation in institutional strength generates both emerging-market and developed-economy outcomes within a unified framework and accounts for heterogeneous post-democratization trajectories in emerging markets.

title: When Do Large Language Models Obey? Evidence on Compliance Across Antisocial and Strategic Domains
affiliations: ESSCA school of management and ESSCA School of Management

detail.title: When Do Large Language Models Obey? Evidence on Compliance Across Antisocial and Strategic Domains
detail.abstract: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) submit to experimenter demand effects in economic decisions as humans do? Using GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Mistral Large, we conduct two experiments comparing model behavior to established human data and test whether minimal, non-binding authority cues shift choices across antisocial and strategic domains. In Study 1, we replicate the Joy of Destruction game to examine compliance with requests to reduce a partner's payoff at a cost to oneself. Models largely resist explicit verbal requests to harm partners, but destruction rises sharply when the same request is embedded in salient procedural structures, such as a clearly labeled decision stage. Adding a brief justification for the request further increases destruction, yielding the highest compliance rates in the study. In Study 2, we implement a one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma following Gächter et al. (2024). While baseline cooperation resembles human patterns, non-binding advisory requests generate large behavioral shifts toward either cooperation or defection. To compare responsiveness across models with different baseline propensities, we introduce a Normalized Directional Compliance index. This reveals a stable ranking across both domains: Mistral Large is most responsive to authority cues, GPT-4o least responsive, and DeepSeek-V3 intermediate. These findings suggest that algorithmic compliance depends less on the linguistic force of an instruction than on its procedural framing, underscoring a susceptibility to influence that persists even in the absence of persuasive argumentation.

title: Adversarial Selection
affiliations: Harvard Law School, Buchman Faculty of Law, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv University and Tel Aviv University

detail.title: Adversarial Selection
detail.abstract: In many institutional settings, k items are selected with the goal of representing the underlying distribution of claims, opinions, or characteristics in a large population. We study environments with two adversarial parties whose preferences over the selected items are commonly known and opposed. We propose the Quantile Mechanism: one party partitions the population into k disjoint subsets, and the other selects one item from each subset. We show that this procedure is optimally representative among all feasible mechanisms, and illustrate its use in jury selection, multi-district litigation, and committee formation.

detail.title: Labor Market rRgidity and Employment: Firm-Level Evidence

detail.abstract: We examine the effect of labor market rigidity on firms' employment decisions in OECD countries using a rich firm-level panel dataset covering 164,048 firm-year observations. Exploiting intertemporal variation in country-level employment protection legislation (EPL), we document a trade-off. While stricter EPL reduces the output sensitivity of firms' employment, it simultaneously lowers firms' overall employment levels. Moreover, our evidence indicates that firms respond to increases in EPL by substituting labor with additional investment in net assets, particularly in labor-intensive industries. Overall, our findings suggest that the level of EPL materially affects firm behavior and that governments should carefully consider the associated trade-offs when designing labor market policies.

detail.abstract: While most of the literature considers economic crisis as a precursor to coup attempts, theoretical considerations suggest that coups may also cause crises. Estimating effects of different types of coups on crisis risk across 32 countries in Latin America and the Caribbean between 1920 and 2022, the findings indicate that civilian-led coups and coups dismantling democracy significantly and substantially increase the likelihood of entering an economic crisis. As such, certain types of coups have severe economic consequences.

detail.abstract: This chapter critically assesses the European Commission's record on enforcing the state aid rules on climate, energy and environmental protection.  It considers the evolution of support for 'energy intensive users' and questions how this policy can be maintained if the objective is to speed up decarbonisation of energy use as well as energy production.  Financial support for fossil fuel production and consumption continues at a high level. Promises to discontinue fossil fuel subsidies are frequently made and rarely kept.

title: A Non-Dictatorial Social Choice Mechanism: A Game-Theoretic Interpretation with Minimal Liberty
affiliations: Calcutta University - Raidighi College

detail.title: A Non-Dictatorial Social Choice Mechanism: A Game-Theoretic Interpretation with Minimal Liberty
detail.abstract: This paper reformulates a non-dictatorial social choice rule within a game-theoretic framework. Individuals are modeled as players whose strategies consist of transitive weak preference relations over a finite set of alternatives. By interpreting a tie between two alternatives as "as good as" rather than indifference, and by replacing the unanimity requirement of Arrow's framework with a weaker condition called minimal liberty, we construct a social outcome function that is transitive, decisive, and non-dictatorial. Minimal liberty ensures that the social outcome strictly reverses no individual's strict preference. The proposed mechanism allows for stable outcomes in the presence of preference disagreement and prevents the concentration of dominant strategic power. This approach offers a bridge between social choice theory and mechanism design, highlighting a balance between individual autonomy and collective rationality.

title: Optimal Annuitization with High Inflation
affiliations: Nottingham University Business School

detail.title: Optimal Annuitization with High Inflation

declarations.funderStatement: This paper received support from Meritz Fire & Marine Insurance Company and the Korea Risk Management Society.

detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic optimal annuitization model incorporating high inflation rates, where an individual determines the optimal time to annuitize. The individual has the right (but not the obligation) to annuitize by entering retirement at some future time of her choosing. We demonstrate that the annuitization decision depends on levels of wealth, which is influenced by the state variable controlling for inflation. The annuitization wealth threshold changes over values of fundamental parameters (e.g., investment opportunity, risk aversion, inflation). We find that when annuitization timing is flexible, the individual tends to extend her working life in response to high inflation rates so that adverse market conditions can be absorbed by delaying annuitization with high wealth thresholds for annuitization.

title: Trading Relationships in FX Derivatives: Lessons from Credit Suisse's Collapse
affiliations: Bank of England and Harvard University

detail.title: Trading Relationships in FX Derivatives: Lessons from Credit Suisse's Collapse
detail.abstract: Using granular transaction-level data, this paper investigates the characteristics and implications of dealer-client trading relationships in the over-the-counter FX derivatives market. We first document that dealer-client trading relationships are persistent over time. Then, to shed light on the role of relationship strength for client access to these instruments during times of dealer stress, we examine the collapse of Credit Suisse in March 2023. In this episode, although Credit Suisse's EURUSD notional traded and trade count declined sharply, clients who had previously relied less heavily on Credit Suisse did not differentially reduce their Credit Suisse-specific trading activity relative to more reliant clients. Instead, clients who had previously relied more heavily on the bank were able to substitute to other existing dealer relationships without incurring additional costs. Overall, these findings suggest that search and bargaining frictions were not particularly costly for heavily reliant clients after the shock: relationship persistence did not differentially prevent them from reallocating activity to existing alternative dealers when their relationship dealer came under stress.

title: The UK Nature Finance Ecosystem: Status and Opportunities for Scale
affiliations: London School of Economics, Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, University of East Anglia (UEA) - School of Environmental Sciences, University of Oxford - Interdisciplinary Centre for Conservation Science,  and University of Oxford

detail.title: The UK Nature Finance Ecosystem: Status and Opportunities for Scale

declarations.funderStatement: Leverhulme Trust; UK Natural Environment Research Council

detail.abstract:
This report provides a comprehensive assessment of the UK’s nature finance landscape, evaluating current financial flows, institutional structures, and the enabling environment required to mobilise investment at scale.  The analysis demonstrates that while public finance remains the dominant source of funding for nature, private finance is already significant but fragmented, difficult to measure, and not yet operating at the scale required. Nature-related financial flows arise through a complex ecosystem of actors, including government, landowners, corporates, financial institutions and philanthropic organisations. These flows take diverse forms, including public subsidies, market-based mechanisms such as biodiversity net gain and carbon markets, private investment (notably in sectors such as water), and emerging financial instruments. However, many existing financial flows continue to drive nature degradation, highlighting the dual challenge of both increasing nature-positive finance and reducing nature-negative investment.

A central contribution of the report is a conceptual framework that distinguishes between “financing green” (mobilising capital for nature-positive activities) and “greening finance” (embedding nature-related risks and impacts into financial decision-making). The findings emphasise that scaling nature finance requires progress on both fronts. It is not simply a question of increasing public expenditure, but of strengthening the broader enabling environment, including policy, regulation, data infrastructure, market design and financial supervision.

The report identifies several critical barriers to scaling private investment. These include weak and uncertain revenue models for nature-based projects, high upfront costs and risks, long investment horizons, limited data and metrics, and policy uncertainty. In particular, the absence of consistent, decision-useful data on nature-related risks and outcomes constrains both investment and risk management. At the same time, the UK is found to lag behind international peers in deploying blended finance mechanisms and leveraging public financial institutions to crowd in private capital.

The report concludes that unlocking nature finance at scale will require coordinated action across four pillars: information and capacity, regulation, financing, and market-based mechanisms. Priorities include strengthening disclosure and supervisory frameworks, improving data and metrics, developing investable project pipelines, and more strategic use of concessional public capital. Taken together, these actions can help align financial flows with environmental goals while supporting growth, resilience and competitiveness in the UK economy.

title: Transitional Justice

detail.title: Transitional Justice
detail.abstract:
Ruti Teitel explores the ways in which a society should respond to evil rule. This is an insightful analysis of one of the most fundamental political science issues of our times - how the emerging democracies in Eastern Europe and elsewhere should deal with the legal systems inherited from their authoritarian pasts.

Should the past system be repudiated altogether? Should the leaders from the authoritarian period be punished? If so, how? Under what principles of law would punishment be justified, given that the leaders were, in general, acting legally according to the legal systems in effect at the time? This book is the first systematic treatment of these issues.

Teitel brings an exceptional breadth of knowledge to bear on the problem, a must read for anyone interested in the role of law in contemporary world politics.

title: Optimism and the Variance Risk Premium
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Boston - Department of Accounting and Finance, University of Alabama - Department of Economics, Finance and Legal Studies, University of Alabama - Department of Economics, Finance and Legal Studies and University of Denver - Daniels College of Business

detail.title: Optimism and the Variance Risk Premium
detail.abstract: We show that market optimism from a representative agent asset pricing model with probability weighting complements and restores the variance risk premium (VRP) in predicting the equity premium. We find the VRP fails to predict stock returns in-sample and out-of-sample. However, introducing optimism derived from a NEO-EU framework along with a positive restricted VRP enhances the predictive power of both variables and forecast encompassing tests reveal that they contain significantly different information in predicting returns. Out-of-sample investment strategies that jointly employ both VRP and optimism generate large Sharpe ratios and abnormal returns. Optimism also complements the VRP in explaining time variation in the stochastic discount factor.

title: The Effects of Universal Preschool in the District of Columbia on Maternal Employment and Population Dynamics
affiliations: George Washington University - Trachtenberg School of Public Policy and Public Administration,  and American University, School of Public Affairs

detail.title: The Effects of Universal Preschool in the District of Columbia on Maternal Employment and Population Dynamics
detail.abstract: Public preschool programs, including the District of Columbia’s universal preschool program, have grown in recent decades. This study uses an event-study approach with data from the American Community Survey (ACS) from 2005 to 2023 to examine the effects of DC’s preschool program on: 1) the share of families with young children in DC; and 2) the labor force participation of mothers with young children in DC, relative to surrounding areas in Maryland and Virginia. Results highlight the changing demographics in DC over this time period. In a triple difference approach, we compare mothers whose youngest child is aged 3 to 4 to those whose youngest child is 6 to 10. Results indicate that DC’s universal preschool program had strong and sustained effects on maternal labor force participation. In the first 14 years of DC pre-K, enrollment in public preschool nearly doubled as did the earnings of mothers with children aged 3 to 4, driven by a 28% increase in their employment and a 4.0 hour per week increase in work hours. There was also some evidence that DC pre-K increased the share of households with a child under age 5 after 10 years. Implications for research and policy are discussed.

title: Transportation Costs, Gravity Model, and International Finance
affiliations: Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University

detail.title: Transportation Costs, Gravity Model, and International Finance
detail.abstract: The gravity model is one of international economics' most celebrated empirical workhorses, yet its fit is systematically imperfect. We argue that a fundamental source of misspecification is the use of great-circle geographic distance, which ignores the stark difference between water-borne and overland transportation costs, terrain barriers, and infrastructure quality. We construct a Transportation-Cost Distance (TCD) measure using granular data on shipping rates, road networks, elevation profiles, AIS vessel-tracking records, and port infrastructure across more than 5,000 sub-national units in 180 countries. Replacing geographic distance with TCD raises gravity-model R 2 by 18-24 percentage points, stabilises the estimated distance elasticity across time (resolving the distance puzzle), and reduces the implied Canada-U.S. border multiplier by nearly half (resolving much of the border puzzle). The gains extend to international finance: TCD substantially improves bilateral equityholdings regressions, home-bias decompositions, and exchange-rate forecasting. Infrastructure quasi-experiments-exploiting 312 major highway, railway, and port openings-provide causal identification and yield an elasticity of trade with respect to TCD of approximately-0.68, consistent with cross-sectional estimates.

title: The Impact of Exchange Rate Depreciation on the Performance of Non-financial Companies in Romania

detail.title: The Impact of Exchange Rate Depreciation on the Performance of Non-financial Companies in Romania

publicationDetails.detailsText: National Bank of Romania Occasional Papers No. 43

detail.abstract: Using a large sample of non-financial companies from Romania, we test whether the major depreciation of the domestic currency that took place in 2008/2009, before the local debut of the Great Recession, had an impact on firm performance through foreign currency indebtedness (to which we refer as “the balance-sheet effect”, in line with the literature). In a difference-in-differences setting, we find that, similar to other countries in the region but for a different set of indicators, the depreciation event had a significantly negative influence on employment and gross value added over the subsequent years. At the same time, the results are heterogeneous in terms of shocks’ transmission to exporters and non-exporting firms. In the former case, the effect is softened by exporters’ foreign currency revenues and increased price competitiveness, or in some specifications statistically insignificant. The results are robust to alternative specifications.

title: Which Intermediary Costs Matter for Asset Prices?
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance, Olin Business School, Washington University in St. Louis and

detail.title: Which Intermediary Costs Matter for Asset Prices?

publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: When intermediaries such as dealers lack the balance-sheet capacity to absorb investor demand, asset prices deviate from fundamentals. Arbitrage spreads (e.g., Treasury-OIS spreads) are widely used to diagnose such distortions. Yet, it is the overall level of prices (e.g., Treasury yields) that ultimately governs borrowing costs and monetary policy transmission, not spreads. It remains unclear whether spreads accurately capture distortions in these levels. We develop a model where intermediaries face two costs: one proportional to portfolio risk, another tied to gross position size. Gross position costs predominantly drive spread distortions; risk costs primarily drive price-level distortions. The theory delivers a sufficient statistic: differences in the rate at which price levels and spreads revert after a demand shock separately identify these costs. We apply this framework to U.S. Treasury and OIS markets using high-frequency demand shocks identified from Treasury auctions. Risk costs dominate on average: demand shocks move yields substantially while leaving spreads largely unchanged. A calibrated model reinforces the disconnect: relaxing position costs such as the supplementary leverage ratio sharply reduces spread volatility with little effect on yield volatility, while easing risk-based costs does the reverse. Overall, spreads alone miss the dominant source of price-level distortions.

title: Learning How To Borrow in a Fintech World: Consumer Behavior When Search Costs Are (Near) Zero
affiliations: Hanken School of Economics and

detail.title: Learning How To Borrow in a Fintech World: Consumer Behavior When Search Costs Are (Near) Zero

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Online loan marketplaces are changing consumer lending. Here we investigate consumer behavior in these markets with near-zero search costs. Using administrative data on 730,000 applications, 750,000 offers, and 200,000 individuals, together with credit registry records, we document four facts. First, substantial within-applicant dispersion in offered terms makes search highly valuable. Second, marketplace nudges mitigate choice complexity. Third, applicants search significantly, applying repeatedly, asking for different terms, and rejecting offers, in ways consistent with their creditworthiness. Fourth, dynamic adverse selection constrains search, as lenders penalize repeat applicants. Our findings highlight trade-offs between informational gains from search, and reputational and cognitive costs.

The analysis continues with the need for investigating the implementation of Total Quality Management in School Units of Special Education. A brief presentation of the Model of Excellence of the European Quality Assurance Agency is also given since this constitutes the basic methodological tool of the research. The research methodology is presented as well as the statistical tools, followed by the results of the statistical analysis and the conclusions. The research findings attribute the significance Leadership and Human Resources as the most prominent quality criteria for the special education school units.

title: Robust Ceo Activism And Two-Sided Alignment: How Elon Musk Gained (And Lost) Legitimacy In The Polarized U.S. News Media Landscape
affiliations: , MBS School of Business and University of Zurich - IBW Department of Business Administration

detail.title: Robust Ceo Activism And Two-Sided Alignment: How Elon Musk Gained (And Lost) Legitimacy In The Polarized U.S. News Media Landscape
detail.abstract: Based on a longitudinal case study of Elon Musk’s sociopolitical activism (2013–2022), we examine the characteristics of chief executive officer (CEO) activism that may enable a CEO to gain legitimacy in an ideologically polarized news media environment. Our study uncovered that, across three phases, Musk’s activism only yielded legitimacy across polarized liberal and conservative news media outlets in the United States in Episode II (2016–2019), whereas in Episodes I (2013–2015) and III (2020–2022), his activism was only aligned with the ideologies and values of one side of the polarized audience (with liberal audiences in Episode I and with conservative audiences in Episode III) but misaligned with the other side. Utilizing inductive theory building and drawing from research on robust action, we develop new theory that distinguishes the influence of what we refer to as robust versus non-robust CEO activism on polarized audiences. Robust CEO activism is constituted by multivocal and diplomatic types of activism, whereas non-robust activism entails univocal and provocative activism. We suggest that robust (rather than non-robust) CEO activism induces ideologically polarized audiences to evaluate a corporate leader coherently and favorably based on a legitimation mechanism which we refer to as two-sided alignment. Our study makes important contributions to different streams of literature and develops normative implications for political conceptions of responsible and ethical leadership.

title: The Strategic Risk of Risk Management and How to Manage It

detail.title: The Strategic Risk of Risk Management and How to Manage It
detail.abstract: The assessment and management of risk-like the valuation and purchase of an asset-is subjective but quantitatively informed, which poses a well-known dichotomy. Perhaps as a result, many executives, Board members and regulators feel they are skilled in the practice of risk management even though relatively few are as evidenced by the numerous risk management failures, which impacted both real and financial assets, over the past decades and which continue to the present day. This paper profiles some of these failures, discusses how risk was allowed to manifest, and why such behavior persists. It then proffers a more practical definition of risk that is not probability-based but instead is a function of error and exposure. The paper then discusses five ways to actively manage risks that pose a threat to a firm's strategic objectives and possibly its existence as a going concern. Such an approach corrects many of the observed risk management issues of the past, which the paper argues is needed given the many observable risks that seem to be developing toward manifestation across the global economy: Political, Economic/Financial, Social, Technological, Environment, and Legal/ Governmental.

title: Misrepresentations of Climate Change as Spiritual and Cultural Crises: The Case of Africa

detail.title: Misrepresentations of Climate Change as Spiritual and Cultural Crises: The Case of Africa
detail.abstract: This study examines the misrepresentation of climate change as a spiritual and cultural phenomenon in African contexts and investigates how such interpretations shape environmental responses and policy outcomes. Drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives from climate studies, cultural analysis, and religious frameworks, the research situates Africa within a paradox of high vulnerability and low historical responsibility for global emissions. It explores how deeply embedded spiritual belief systems, ranging from indigenous cosmologies to syncretic Christian and Islamic practices, serve as interpretive lenses through which climatic events are understood, often attributing environmental disruptions to divine will, ancestral forces, or supernatural causality. While these belief systems historically promote ecological harmony and conservation practices, the study argues that their misinterpretation can foster fatalism, weaken scientific engagement, and impede adaptive climate action. Through qualitative synthesis of case studies across African regions, including droughts, floods, and deforestation crises, the research highlights how structural inequalities, colonial legacies, and governance challenges intersect with cultural narratives to complicate climate responses. The study calls for a reframing of climate communication strategies that integrate, rather than dismiss, spiritual worldviews while correcting distortions that hinder action. By bridging scientific knowledge with culturally grounded epistemologies, it proposes a more context-sensitive approach to climate engagement that enhances policy effectiveness and community resilience across the continent.

title: Designing Lifecycle-Based Digital Work Permit Governance Systems To Prevent Regulatory Lapses In Uganda's NGO Sector

detail.title: Designing Lifecycle-Based Digital Work Permit Governance Systems To Prevent Regulatory Lapses In Uganda's NGO Sector
detail.abstract: Regulatory compliance with work permit requirements remains a persistent challenge for nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) operating in Uganda, often resulting in legal penalties, operational disruptions, and risks to organizational licensing. These challenges are largely driven by fragmented compliance processes, limited coordination between regulatory institutions, and the absence of integrated systems for managing expatriate workforce authorization. This study addresses these gaps by proposing a lifecycle-based, ERP-integrated governance framework designed to prevent regulatory lapses and enhance compliance within Uganda's NGO sector.

detail.abstract: As the Middle East enters a phase of kinetic escalation following the February 2026 regional shocks, Pakistan finds itself caught in a "Geographic Vice"—a terminal state of strategic paralysis between its primary financial creditors in the GCC and its volatile, intertwined security border with Iran. This paper examines the systemic collapse of Pakistan’s "Strategic Ambiguity" doctrine under the weight of contradictory defense pacts: the 2014/2024 Iranian Security Pacts and the 2025 Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) with Riyadh. By mapping the crisis across five structural nodes—Sovereignty, Macroeconomics, Asymmetric Attrition, Demographic Polarization, and the Normalization Trap—the analysis argues that yielding to external pressure for military or logistical intervention presents a high probability of irreversible domestic collapse. Ultimately, the paper proposes a pivot toward "Strategic Maneuverability" through five actionable micro-policy compromises, asserting that Pakistan’s survival depends on its ability to transition from a transactional proxy to an intact, nuclear-armed mediator.

title: It Takes Two to Tango: The Role of Client Contribution in Shaping Audit Outcomes
affiliations: Tilburg University, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, VU University Amsterdam and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: It Takes Two to Tango: The Role of Client Contribution in Shaping Audit Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Ivan Hagenbeek is employed by and has research support from Deloitte Netherlands. Anna Gold serves as the Academic Director of the Foundation for Auditing Research in the Netherlands. Bart Dierynck and Christian P.H. Peters have no financial conflicts of interest related to this research.

detail.abstract: Regulatory frameworks and the professional service literature emphasize that audit quality depends on effective cooperation between auditors and their clients. However, empirical evidence on how client contribution shapes audit outcomes remains limited. We address this gap by leveraging a novel engagement-level measure of client contribution based on auditors’ assessments. Combining survey data from 210 auditors with proprietary archival data from a Big 4 audit firm, we examine the association between client contribution and audit quality, efficiency, and behavioral outcomes. We find that higher client contribution is associated with improved audit quality, reflected in greater detection of material misstatements, higher perceived audit process quality, and a lower likelihood of meeting or beating earnings benchmarks. Further, higher client contribution is associated with greater audit efficiency as well as lower perceived complexity and workload pressure. Overall, our findings highlight the meaningful role of clients as co-producers of audit outcomes.

title: Designing Second-Best Price Zones in Electricity Markets
affiliations: and Technische Universität München (TUM)

detail.title: Designing Second-Best Price Zones in Electricity Markets
detail.abstract: In electricity markets, marginal costs vary substantially across space and time, implying welfare losses under spatially or temporally uniform pricing. In practice, prices are typically aggregated into large zones with spatially uniform prices. This paper develops an empirical framework to quantify the welfare loss of zonal pricing and to design welfare-improving price zones. We propose the spatial R-squared as a measure of spatial market efficiency and show that economically motivated clustering methods recover efficiency-maximizing zones. Applying the framework to three U.S. wholesale electricity markets, we demonstrate its computational tractability and find that existing zones are misaligned with current network conditions.

title: The Impact of Feedback, Verbal Rewards, and Job Value on Employee Satisfaction
affiliations: Warsaw School of Economics

detail.title: The Impact of Feedback, Verbal Rewards, and Job Value on Employee Satisfaction
detail.abstract: Research on the factors influencing job satisfaction has a long tradition. Based on Herzberg's theory, research on the impact of motivators and hygiene factors on satisfaction is experiencing a renaissance in management science. Positive feedback, in turn, increases intrinsic motivation by satisfying the needs for competence and autonomy, leading to stronger commitment and job satisfaction. The honesty of feedback also increases motivation to improve performance and thus increases job satisfaction. Therefore, this study seeks to answer two research questions. First, will Herzberg's theory be positively verified empirically? Second, what is the impact of supervisors' verbal behaviors on their subordinates' job satisfaction? Three groups of motivational and hygiene factors were examined: (1) security and conditions, (2) status and rewards, and (3) personal development and stimulation. The honesty of feedback and verbal rewards from supervisors were also examined. A quantitative study was conducted on a group of employees from various companies (N=145). The impact of work values on job satisfaction was partially confirmed. The negative impact of hygiene factors on job satisfaction was empirically confirmed. In turn, verbal rewards from superiors and honest feedback had a significant impact on increasing job satisfaction. Practical implications were proposed.

title: Noise, Selection, and the Illusion of Bias: Why Unbiased Estimates Produce Systematic Cost Overruns

detail.title: Noise, Selection, and the Illusion of Bias: Why Unbiased Estimates Produce Systematic Cost Overruns

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author provides consulting services to Oxford Global Projects (OGP), a consultancy specializing in infrastructure project risk and cost estimation. The analytical framework presented here has implications for reference class forecasting methods, including those used in consultancy practice. The analysis and results were developed independently as part of the author's PhD research at Aarhus University.

detail.abstract: Infrastructure projects consistently exhibit cost overruns and benefit shortfalls, a pattern widely attributed to optimism bias or strategic misrepresentation. This paper shows that a simpler mechanism -- the interaction between estimation noise and selection on estimated benefit-cost ratios -- can account for much of the observed pattern. I derive closed-form expressions for the expected cost overrun in a portfolio of projects selected by ranking on noisy benefit-cost ratios, drawing on the econometrics of sample selection (Heckman, 1979) and the winner's curse (Capen, Clapp, and Campbell, 1971). The key result is that the expected cost overrun for selected projects is approximately exp(σ²_c λ(Φ⁻¹(1-α))/√(σ²_c + σ²_b)), where σ_c and σ_b are the noise levels in cost and benefit estimation and λ is the inverse Mills ratio of the selection threshold. Monte Carlo simulations confirm the analytical predictions. Calibrating the model to a noise level consistent with AACE Class 3 cost estimates (σ ≈ 0.20), I find that the selection mechanism can account for 20-80% of empirically observed overruns across eight infrastructure categories, with the largest explanatory share for roads (80%) and the smallest for dams (20%). These findings imply that de-biasing adjustments calibrated to observed overruns may overcorrect, and that improving estimation precision reduces overruns even absent bias correction.

title: Government Employment Shocks, Policy Coordination, and Debt Structure
affiliations: Towson University, Texas State University and Auburn University

detail.title: Government Employment Shocks, Policy Coordination, and Debt Structure
detail.abstract: This paper provides a unified explanation for the historically varying labor-market effects of government employment shocks in the United States. Using a Bayesian SVAR with max-share identification, we document three postwar episodes: public hiring crowded in private employment, raised real wages, and reduced unemployment in the pre-Volcker era; became contractionary during the Great Moderation; and was largely ineffective after the Global Financial Crisis. To explain these shifts, we develop a New Keynesian DSGE model with alternative monetary-fiscal regimes and government debt structures. The model features fiscal-monetary coordination in both the pre-Volcker and post-GFC periods, but under sharply different debt durations. Longer debt maturities weaken fiscal transmission-even under passive monetary policy-by dampening real interest rate and debt-revaluation wealth effects, while aggressive anti-inflationary policy, as in the Great Moderation, renders government employment shocks contractionary regardless of debt maturity.

detail.abstract: Economics as a discipline maintains an institutional posture against prescriptive work, yet preliminary survey data suggests that roughly 90 percent of the public believe economists should play some role in shaping economic policy. This is not a study of policy preferences or redistributive attitudes, but of prescriptive modality. Asking explicitly what role the public believes economists ought to play in the policy process. Using a nationally representative survey of U.S. adults conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago through the AmeriSpeak panel, this paper presents the first nationally representative evidence on public expectations of economists' professional obligations. We find that a majority support economists recommending or advocating for policies, while most prefer collaborative rather than expert-led goal-setting. Future work will extend this agenda through surveys of economists themselves, examining whether professional practice aligns with, or diverges from, the public perceptions. These results contribute to research on expertise, legitimacy, and public trust, and carry practical implications for how economists communicate policy in public-facing work.

title: Politically Coded: CEO Partisanship and Firm AI Adoption
affiliations: Belk College of Business, UNC Charlotte,  and

detail.title: Politically Coded: CEO Partisanship and Firm AI Adoption
detail.abstract: Using FEC political donation records to measure CEO partisanship and job posting data from Revelio Labs to measure corporate AI adoption, we document a robust partisan gap: firms led by Republican-leaning CEOs devote a smaller share of their hiring to AI than those led by Democratic-leaning CEOs. Instrumental variable estimation exploiting the partisan composition of the local CEO labor market suggests a causal interpretation. Restricting to CEOs appointed before AI became a corporate priority produces similar results. The partisan gap concentrates in high AI-exposure industries and persists even when peers are visibly adopting AI. We also find that appointing a Republican-leaning CEO in a high AI-exposure industry during the post-AI era is associated with negative abnormal announcement returns of approximately 2.5 percentage points.

title: Second-best Monopoly Pricing in a Congested Service System
affiliations: University of Haifa, Tel Aviv University - Coller School of Management and University of Haifa

detail.title: Second-best Monopoly Pricing in a Congested Service System
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: We study pricing and regulation in a congested service system operated by a profit-maximizing monopolist, where access to a privately owned service can be priced while a public alternative remains free. This setting arises naturally in markets that combine private and public provision, such as transportation networks with tolled lanes and free roads or healthcare systems with private and public service tiers. Such environments are inherently "second best": pricing decisions at the private service affect not only paying customers but also congestion experienced by users of the free alternative, while institutional or legal constraints limit the ability to price the public channel. This interdependence creates a central regulatory challenge: how should access be controlled when monopoly pricing in one part of the system generates spillover congestion elsewhere?
Methodology/results: We develop a stylized model in which strategic customers choose, based on price and waiting costs, between two M/M/1 queues: a priced server operated by a revenue-maximizing monopolist and a free alternative. We characterize equilibrium outcomes under monopoly pricing and compare them with both the socially optimal allocation and the unregulated, free access case. Monopoly pricing distorts system performance by restricting access to the priced server and shifting congestion to the free server, exploiting cross-server congestion spillovers. As a result, monopoly pricing can lead to higher social cost not only relative to the social optimum but even compared to unregulated access, and the inefficiency gap can become arbitrarily large. We then introduce a simple regulatory mechanism—the q-control mechanism—that requires a fixed fraction q of customers to be admitted at a regulated price. This mechanism reshapes the monopolist’s incentives by limiting its ability to extract revenue through congestion spillovers. We characterize how the optimal choice of q depends on system parameters and show that the mechanism can mitigate monopoly distortions and even restore the first-best outcome.
Managerial implications: Our findings highlight the key limitations of relying on monopoly pricing to manage congestion in second-best service systems with mixed public–private provision, where pricing tools are institutionally constrained. When pricing power is concentrated in the hands of a single operator, tolls may be used not only to ration access but also to shift
congestion toward unpriced alternatives, worsening overall performance. Rather than regulating prices directly or subsidizing capacity, regulators can improve efficiency by shaping the composition of demand. In particular, price concessions—often introduced for equity—can also serve as an operational tool: guaranteeing a fraction of users access at regulated terms can discipline monopoly incentives, reduce congestion spillovers, and improve system performance.

title: Approximations to Stockout-based Substitution under MNL Model
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), Antai College of Economics and Management and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

detail.title: Approximations to Stockout-based Substitution under MNL Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
We study a finite-horizon inventory planning problem in which a retailer chooses initial stocking quantities for multiple products before a sequence of customer arrivals, and customers substitute among products according to a multinomial logit (MNL) choice model when stockouts occur. The dynamic substitution induced by inventory depletion creates complex dependencies among product sales, making both analysis of the sales process and optimization of stocking decisions challenging. 

We first analyze the sales process itself. Using a continuous-time embedding, we present the discrete-time substitution dynamics through capped Poisson processes whose evolution is governed by a stopping time corresponding to the depletion of inventory capacity. This representation yields an exact characterization of expected sales and enables a Gaussian approximation of the sales process. We show that the resulting approximation yields uniformly bounded errors in expected sales, and importantly, allows substantially more efficient simulation compared with the original stochastic system. 

Building on this analytical framework, we then study the retailer's inventory planning problem. We revisit the fluid relaxation that reduces to a static assortment optimization problem and show that a simple rounding procedure achieves an O(√ T) optimality gap that is independent of the number of products, improving existing guarantees. We further develop a diffusion-scale refinement that captures stochastic fluctuations around the fluid solution and reduces the optimization problem to one whose optimality gap relative to the original problem is a constant. Numerical experiments demonstrate that solutions obtained from this diffusion approximation substantially improve upon the rounded fluid solution.

detail.abstract: Across the social sector, the language of impact is ubiquitous, and leaders increasingly speak of achieving "lasting" or "enduring" impact in recognition that durable outcomes matter more than short-term gains. Yet many organizations that deliver meaningful and impactful products, services and programs remain structurally fragile and become destabilized when funding contracts, political priorities shift or leadership transitions occur. This article argues for intentionally design organizations for durability from the moment they are launched, treating volatility as a baseline condition rather than an occasional disruption. These enduring impact organizations embed governance architecture, financial diversification, succession planning and strong cultural systems to preserve mission fidelity and operational capacity across decades of change.

The unit explains how corporate communication supports organizations in four key areas: managing crises, engaging stakeholders, behaving ethically, and handling the media. It first introduces crisis management concepts and then illustrates them through detailed analyses of the Infosys leadership crisis and the Nestlé Maggi noodles controversy in India, highlighting what worked and what failed in their communication strategies. detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolution of Canada's medicalized immigration exclusion from 1902-1965, tracing how rudimentary physical inspections morphed into targeted parasitological and radiological screening targeting Chinese, Hindu, and South Asian migrants. Through Inspector G.W. Skenler's Vancouver protocols-buttonhook trachoma exams, triple stool purges for hookworm (Necator americanus), and phthisis pulmonalis X-rays-the state operationalized biological border sovereignty, rejecting 41% of "Oriental" applicants for ova-positive stools or corneal pannus. Personal vignettes-a 1960s Indian immigrant's London digital rectal exam and Ontario false-positive TB (Ghon complex) treated with 100-day isoniazid prophylaxis-reveal persistence two decades post-Chinese Immigration Act repeal. Key argument: Medical inadmissibility achieved what quotas could not, embedding racial parasitology in IRCC procedure. Digital rectal trauma, thymol purges, and LTBI overdiagnosis persisted as "public charge" proxies, modernizing Senkler's 1910 66% Hindu hookworm fiction into 1960s 92% South Asian DRE reality. title: State-Substitute Governance in Armed Conflict:The Formation, Maintenance and Boundaries of Accountability of the Detention System in North-Eastern Syria
